chemical means of production.

During this period of activity in manufac-
tures how did our working men fare? What
may be called small mastership ceased. The
huge, complicated, and expensive machinery
of the factory destroyed the simple manufac-
turing contrivances of the cottage. There
only remained workers and great masters, and
as the workers were being in many oases super-
seded by the machines, and as machinery, by
its rapid extension, furnished the means of
periodical over-supply, pauperism became the
only resource of the unemployed, the aged,
the feeble, and the improvident. Associative
effort might have been resorted to by the
workers as a remedy for the evils under which
they suffered. Even at this early period of
our manufacturing industry, trades unions
and co-operative associations might have
forced better wages from employers, and given
the many the means by united capital to reap
some of the advantages which, as industrious
and honest men, the workers were fairly en-
titled to. The law, however, with a diabolical
iniquity, interfered to prevent this. The fears
of a bad Government and the jealousies of
dominant classes by aid of the law made all
attempts at associative action for trade or other
purposes criminal. Our working men could
not combine for any purpose in connection
with their labour without becoming liable to
fine or imprisonment; nor were our highly
skilled artizans free to emigrate; and thus the
efforts by which they are now improving their
condition, by being made criminal, became
necessarily impossible. Thus the marvellous
influx of wealth brought by our industry
flowed into the coffers of a limited number,
whilst the masses of those who laboured to
produce it had no power to touch or enjoy
even the overflowings of its abundance.
Our ingenious men invented machines, our
industrious men worked them, our productive
power came to have no practical limit. We
had studied how to produce, and had suc-
ceeded, but our statesmen and politicians had
taken no thought as to individual or national
equity in distribution. We have, therefore,
surfeit on one hand, and hunger on the other.
Millionaires with heaps of unnecessary wealth,
and workers hungering in our streets and
fields with no ultimate resource but the work-
house. The list given in the Spectator of the
few very lucky individuals, whose personalty
was above 12.50,000, and who have died within
the last ten years, left in the gross about GO mil-
lions sterling. Whilst, if we turn to that other
list, which gives the number and cost of our
paupers, we find a counterpart awful enough
in its character to strike the heart of the most
cheerful optimist with dismay. Estimated at
the lowest, we have not, for the last ten years,
had less than a million paupers on our hands,
to say nothing of the miserable suffering mul-
titudes who have not yet passed into that hideous
category. During the same ten years these
paupers have cost at least 7 millions a year, or
70 millions sterling as a grand total.

Let the producers of the country's wealth—
the workers—put these two sums together, ab-
stractions from labour by the rich on the one
hand, and hy the poor on the other, and they will
have some idea as to the way in which the in-
dustrial energies of the country are weighted,
pressed upon by exactions, which make the
artizan's meals scant, and the field labourer's
couditiou one of almost continual famine.

How this marvellous growth of our manufac-
turing system has affected the prosperity of
the landowners is too long a story to tell here.
We know that land has become a luxury, that
its price has gone up in consequence, and that
the grandeur Of those few who have bought
themselves into its almost exclusive possession
surpasses anything known in the world since
ADA.Ii was driven through the portals of Para-
dise. It is making no attack on property to
say that the contrast between excessive wealth
and extreme poverty is at this hour in England
a reproach, a scandal, a danger. It implies
stupid and dishonest government, and it
means the employment of law, custom, and
intelligence as agencies for the plunder of the
masses. Good government means the pursuit
of policies calculated to promote the general
welfare of the people—to secure permanent
good by wisely utilizing temporary di faculties—
by aiming at the promotion of industry in its
highest, best, and. most fruitful forms—and
having done so, by labouring to_secure such a
distribution of it as shall secure, at least, a
moderate degree of comfort and happiness to
those whose honest toil has given us such
abundance.

It is the merest nonsense to boast of the
wealth of a nation in which the masses of the
people have no security for the commonest
neaessaries of life from one day to another.
The very fact that at the moment when
prosperity is at its highest, millions of workers
should he crying piteously for as much bread
as will keep life in them and their families as
a return for their labour, is of itself enough to
condemn, without right of appeal, a system of
things which is a practical outrage on the
justice and wisdom of the CREATOR.
There is no use in trying to hide the fact
that we are in the midst of danger—that such
a system as ours, with its shocking social
anomalies, necessarily carries danger in it.
Woe to the nation where the magnificence of
the few displays itself in the face of the misery
of the many ; and that woo will most assuredly
come to England, unless her statesmen can
discover some way of rectifying so disgraceful,
so inhuman a condition of things, or if the
masses of her people, made wise by their
sufferings, do not set themselves quietly and
thoughtfully to work, with the view of putting
a higher spirit of justice into the business of
life. It may be pleasant to know that a
favoured few can count their millions of
acquired wealth, but it is most certainly not
safe to do so in the presence of miserable
masses of men who, under the excitement of
their miseries, have little to count but their
wrongs. What Mr. GLADSTONE and the higher
few by whom he is surrounded can do to steer
clear of the danger ahead, it is difficult to
say. How poor pettifoggers like A YRTON can
destroy the calmness and the social agreement
necessary, whilst dealing with such difficulties,
we are made more painfully aware of daily.

articles.title: OUR MILLIONAIRES AND OUR WORKERS.
articles.text:
OUR MILLIONAIRES AND OUR
WORKERS.

Tun Spectator of last Saturday contained
a list, extracted from the files of the Illustrated
London News, of fortunes, a quarter of a
million sterling, upwards, left by deceased
persons during the last ten years. The
figures are all round numbers, fifty thousand
being the stride always taken, except in two
or three instances, so that many hundreds of
thousands must have been dropped out; and
when it is remembered that .the enormous
sums stated only refer to personality, it will
be easily understood that, largo as the figures
are, they only represent a portion actually
possessed by these wonderfully wealthy per-
sons. It must not be forgotten that all under
£250,000 are omitted, put by as nobodies;
but, at the same time, it may be said, that
this multitude of comparatively poor persons
must have absorbed an almost incalculable
amount of the country's wealth.
We can understand, after considering this,
and studying the list before us, how true the
saying is, that "England is the richest
country in the world." That wealthy people
are more numerous in England
.than in any
other country on the face of the earth. But we
cannot understand so easily why it is,
.that,
at the same time, England is the. Poorest
country in the world. That is, a larger num-
ber of people, in proportion to its population,
have sunk into the lowest and most despairing
depths of pauperism in England than any-
where else on the surface of the rOund globe.
We can account for the growth of the wealth
of England by the development of mechanical
and chemical science applied to
.manufactures.
A knowledge of this explains the increase in
every branch of manufacturing.industry, and
a monopoly of these sources Of wealth in the
hands of a comparative few , makes it clear
why our manufacturers have become million-
aires, whilst such masses of • our operatives
remain on the verge of pauperism.
Towards the close of last century a few well-
timed inventions gave birth to our gigantic
factory system; those who possessed capital,
knowledge of business, and some degree of
experience or education, then stepped in, took
possession of the field, and rapidly became the
possessors of enormous wealth. The laws were
so framed as to encourage individual energy
and enterprise ; and it must be confessed in-
dividual energy and enterprise were perfectly
successful in bringing wealth into the country.
Hence naturally great individual fortunes.
The possession of thirty, forty, or fifty thou-
sand pounds ceased to satisfy the ambition of
our manufacturers, and the list before us points
to millions in many eases produced by simple

Some people regard this impudent travesty

desire to see the memories of great men

articles.title: EVILS OF CANVASSERS AT ELECTIONS.
articles.text:
THE EVILS OF CANVASSERS AT
ELECTIONS.

PAID canvassers at elections are, no doubt,
a very great evil, besides being an annoy-
ance and a nuisance, but there are a certain
class of unpaid canvassers that are a great deal
more so. The fact is, paid canvassers for the
most part are a mere lot of hirelings, who care
very little what candidate be returned so that
they receive their pay. Whereas, the really
earnest, most corrupting and demoralizing
canvassers are the members of unscrupulous
men of wealth and influence, who go round
among those over whom they know they have
control, and extort promises from them. In
the rural districts this system of coercion is
practical to such an extent as to render the
freedom of election impossible, even with the
Ballot. No sooner is an election announced
to take place than the squirearchy, the par-
sons, the agents of the principal landlords,
and others of influence, form themselves into
a committee, and then divide into sections,
and sally forth to commence their coercive
canvass, and operate upon tradesmen in the
surrounding villages, tenant farmers, work-
men, and any other electors they can lay their
unclean hands upon, and literally besiege the
houses and persons of these unhappy electors
until they worry them into a promise to vote
as these men wish them. The election agent,
who is generally a lawyer, and the small
fry of paid agents under him, are very insigni-
ficant individuals compared to the great un-
paid canvassers, who, for the most part, have
the power of injuring, and in some eases
ruining, any man of independent mind whom
they would look upon as a refractory elector
Now, while canvassing of this kind is per-
mitted and reduced to a system, neither the
Ballot nor any other contrivance will ever
secure freedom of election. The same system
prevails to a greater or lesser extent in borough
elections. • It is very well know,i the late
elections at Preston and Tiverton were decided
in favour of the respective candidates by the
unscrupulous and determined canvass that
was carried on in the factories and workshops
of partizan employers in each town. And so
far as .can be learned this was not done so
much
.by paid canvassers as by managers,
foremen, and understrappers, currying favour
with their employers, and if a law was passed
to-morrow to prevent paid canvassing it would
.never reach these worthies, nor the great
at elections.
unpaid, whose name is legion;

Now, it was with a view of reaching these
unpaid patriots, that I moved a resolu-
tion at the Electoral Reform Conference,
lately held in St. James's Hall, to the effect
"That no electoral reform can be complete
which does not provide for the prevention of
systematic canvassing as practised in factories,
workshops, house-to-house, and personal can-
vass, and that all such canvassing be made a
misdemeanour, punishable with imprison-
ment." I pity the simplicity of any man who
levels a resolution, or fires a squib against paid
canvassers, and yet allows the great unpaid
electioneering malefactors to remain un-
punished.

Speaking of paid canvassers, who is to prove
paid agency? These agents arc generally
moro knaves than fools, and are not likely to
criminate themselves, and therefore any pro-
vision against paid canvassers would be of
little use. It is against canvassing in any
way or form that provision ought to be made.
The platform and the press are the only fair,
just, and legitimate electioneering agents that
ought to be employed. What right has any
set of men to enter another man's house, or in
any way approach his person, and request the
surrender of his judgment, and become his
keeper? If we prefer one candidate to another
as the representative of certain principles,
surely it is enough to advocate his claims upon
the platform, or through the press in various
ways, such as posters, pamphlets, and news-
papers, without worrying men to death to
coerce them to promise their votes. But per-
haps we may be told the Ballot will protect the
voter against this. The Ballot will do nothing
of the kind, unaccompanied with other pro-
tective measures. Moreover, a vast number of
electors have not confidence as yet in the
secrecy of the Ballot. They are frightened
and bullied into the belief that those who
have power over them will be sure to know
how they have voted. That was the object in
view in the Preston "card trick," the men
having been canvassed and frightened into the
belief that if they did not give up their cards
they would be sure to be found out. Timo
will, no doubt, rectify this; but so long as we
permit men to be coerced into promising their
votes, they do not like to run the risk of vio-
lating their promise, and although the Ballot
is as secret as the tomb, the electors must be
made certain of this; and, in addition, make
canvassing a misdemeanour, punishable with
imprisonment, and then we shall have freedom
of election, but not before.

articles.title: ALFRED A. WALTON.
articles.text:
ALFRED A. WALTON.

THE CO-OPERATIVE SYSTEM.

Mn. 112sniusoN, when remarking that " co-
operation is in no position to transform the
whole condition of industry, and to give us a
new social future,' should state distinctly the
form of co-operation to which he refers. If
he speaks of co-operative stores and partner-
ships of industry, the renmrk is superfluous.
But although co-operation, while it is restricted
to these very imperfect applications of it, will
never give us a new social future, it will lead
to the practical initiation by the working
classes of the complete system which will give
a new feature to the human race, and which
alone can put things right in the social world,
if, to the eternal disgrace of the present more
wealthy and educated classes, this universally
beneficent reform is allowed to be practically
initiated by means of funds provided by their
poorer and less educated fellow men. The
knowledge required for the realization of this
change (the knowledge of the causes of evil
and of good to man, in the formation of cha-
racter, in the production and distribution of
wealth, and in social arrangements and pro-
ceedings in general, which is the only basis
upon which the intellectual and moral character
necessary for the realization of effectual social
reform can be attained), having now been suffi-
ciently prepared for practical application, it
remains to be seen whether the working
classes, or the more educated and wealthy, will
be the first to acquire it and to apply it prac-
tically. It remains to be seen whether the
working classes, with their limited means and
powers, shall be left to their own exertions to
realize the practical initiation of the new sys-
tem, or whether a few of the more intelligent
and benevolent and justly disposed of those

who at present are less unfavourably placed,
and who are possessed of more capability for
the direction of extensive practical measures,
can be induced to acquire the new knowledge
and enlightened feelings so far as to take the
matter in hand from the first. Men of this
class will take it up quickly enough when they
know what it is, as the members of the Civil
Service have taken up co-operative store-keep-
ing; and it will bring to all who enter into it a
thousand immense advantages where co-opera-
tive stores can only bring them a few compara-
tively unimportant benefits. And there must
be very many who, without waiting for prac-
tical demonstration, may acquire the new
knowledge, and who, if they could be induced
to do so, would be able to divest themselves of
the moral infirmities by which they are now
caused to cling to a system thoroughly incon-
sistent with all enlightened ideas of the duties
of man to man, and scarcely, if at all, less in-
jurious to the middle and upper classes than
to the working classes and to the very poor.
Men of every class may surely understand
that a system composed entirely of causes of
good, in man's intellectual and moral character
and in his surrounding, must be infinitely
better for all than the present chaotic aggre-
gate of causes of evil, mental, material, and
practical, can possibly be for the most favoured
ndividuals, or, rather, for those who are the
east injured by it. And the highest useful
talents and true refinement which the present
system has produced will find their best appli-
cation in the practical development of the new
system, from which ultimately all that is in-
ferior in the human character and in sur-
rounding objects will be as much as possible
excluded.

It matters little what name is given to the
new system; but it is very important that it
should be clearly distinguished from every
idea of social reform which is not perfectly
consistent with goodwill to all, and which
is not based upon the knowledge of
the causes of evil and of good to man,
and upon the spirit of enlightened
goodness which this knowledge alone can
produce. There arc many forms of "socialism,"
in which there is no indication whatever of
this knowledge, and which include a variety
of ideas totally inconsistent with it. Mr.
OwErr, in fact, the discoverer of the new
knowledge, is the only leading social reformer
in whose writings the basis upon which alone
an effective system of social reform can be
constructed is to be found; and in these the
new knowledge is so falsified by the error
which I have corrected (see BEE-HITE, Nov.
2 and 9), that it could not be made intelli-
gible, and was always open to hostile criticism
which could not be refuted. And yet he had
verified it practically in a most admirable
manner in his great experiment at New
Lanark. As a worker, in verifying the truth
which is the basis of the new knowledge, he
was most successful; because in this he was
applying a true fundamental idea. But as a
teacher of his pAnciples and system he was
most unsuccessful ; because in all that be
said and wrote he constantly reiterated his
fundamental error and the false inferences to
which it leads, in the place of his funda-
mental truth and the true inferences which
follow from it when it is combined with the
corrective truth, which in his fundamental
error ho denied. Now that this obstacle to the
dissemination of the new knowledge is re-
moved, the success in making it generally
known will certainly be obtained in due time,
which was denied to the life-long exertions of
the man to whom the world is indebted for
the greatest discovery which has been made
in the history of humanity, for the good of
mankind—the discovery which will mark the
commencement of a new era in the destiny of
man.

There will be no difficulty in adjusting the
minor details of the new system under the
guidance of the general knowledge of the
causes of evil and of good and of the spirit of
the system; but it is of little us to discuss
them where this knowledge and spirit .are
absent. The new knowledge must be studied,
as any other important subject must be, and
men must understand it from its foundation,
before there can be the agreement of opinion
respecting it which always exists in reference

to knowledge of any kind among those who
possess it. • There will, of course, be perfect
agreement upon all essential points among
those who acquire this knowledge. And the
dissent of those who do not possess it cannot
have the least influence with those who have
it, except to cause them to regret the want of
knowledge of the dissentients, and to endeavour
to induce them to study the subject until they
understand it. (The astronomer is uninfluenced
by the man who thinks that the earth is flat
and the sun goes round it.) The social reformer
wtio neglects to make himself master of this
subject is in this neglect an enemy to himself
and to all who are so unfortunate as to be
influenced by him in the forming of their
views.

This, then, is the reply, briefly, to Mr.
limutisoN's enquiry for the "orthodox co-
operation." The societies by whom it is
realized will "depart hence," as Mr. JONES
says, in the sense that they will form new
arrangements, apart from those of the present
system, but in friendly relations with them,
in which they will produce and distribute
wealth, educate, and regulate their social pro-
ceedings, in accordance with true enlighten-
ment and enlightened goodness. Afy little
pamphlet and tract, advertised on page 8, are
intended to give brief descriptions of this
subject in its three chief divisions.

articles.title: HENRY TRAVIS.
articles.text:
HENRY TRAVIS.

THE HOMES OF THE LONDON POOR.

On Friday morning a deputation, consisting
of Dr. Bennett, Dr. Gibbon, Messrs. A. N.
Phillips, J. P., Alexander Rivington, Brooke,
Henry Clarke, J. Walker, George Sopron,.
Win. Lovell, and Wm. Catlin, waited on the
Lord Mayor at the Mansion House, with respect
to the wholesale demolition of houses of the
poor in the metropolis, more especially in the
vicinity of Clerkenwell. The deputation was
introduced by Sir John Bennett, who add.ress.ed
his lordship, laying before him the injustice
and cruelty inflicted on the poorer classes by
the demolition of houses to make way for new
streets, &c., without provision being made for
the accommodation of those persons who were
thereby ejected.
The Lord Mayor expressed the great
pleasure which it gave him to receive the
deputation, the presence of which was the best
possible evidence of the interest taken in the
movement to provide suitable dwellings for
the working classes. The committee of which
he was a member had induced Mr. Bruce. to
have a clause inserted in a recent act of Parlia-
ment compelling the Metropolitan Board to set
apart spaces for the dwellings of the poor in
place of those which they had deprived them
of in making street improvements; but the
board would not allow the Improved Industrial
Dwellings Committee to have anything to do
with the selection of the sites. However, they
had done the best they could in inducing
Parliament to recognise the claims of the work-
ing classes in this particular. As to the want
of money for the erection of such improved
dwellings, he could assure them that there
would be no difficulty in obtaining the necessary
funds. If they were building for the future
, they must erect such buildings as the men of
the future would be satisfied with—houses in
which a man could rear his family with that
moral and religious teaching which was the
basis of a pure and successful career in life.
As to cheap trains enabling men to live out of
the town, lie beleived that such was being done
by some of the railway companies, and that
the acoommodation would be regulated by the
demand. He believed, however, that the
proper thing was to have dwellings erected
for workine men within easy reach of their
work. • If a man was the sole bread-winner
for the family, and had settled hours for em-
ployment, it might be advantageous to him to
live out of town, but it was otherwise with
the great majority, the members of whose
families grown up increased by their earnings
the general fund, and for such it was most
desirable to have their dwellings within easy
reach of their work. In conclusion, his
lord-
ship assured the deputation that he kePt
constant watch over the question, and heas
begged them if they ever thought it win
his power to be of any assistance never to
hesitate for a moment in applying to him.
Sir John Bennett having returned thanks
on behalf of those present for the courteous
reception they had met with at the hands of
his lordship, the deputation withdrew.

From April Ist to the 16th inst. the Trea-
sury receipts amounted to £420525,883-70
increase of about two millions and a halt as
compared with the corresponding period ef
last year. The expenditure has been
£44,337,677. On Saturday last the balance
in the Bank of England was X 4,329,058, ani
in that of Ireland £1,068,126.

articles.title: METROPOLITAN POLICE.
articles.text:
THE METROPOLITAN POLICE.

On the 16th inst. Constable 466 P, or Camber-
'well, division, Henry Goodehild was reported to
the Commissioner for insubordination in positively
refusing to obey the orders of the District and
Divisional Superintendents to remove to a different
part of his division. The case was heard, we are
informed, in the usual way, and, upon the dis-
obedience being fully established, the Assistant-
Commissioner, Colonel Labalmondiere, dismissed
the constable for this offence against the regula-
tions of the service. Goodchild at once visited or
telegraphed to the so-called delegates, to whom he
had, it appears, acted as secretary of each division,.
stating that he was dismissed, that he had seen
six divisions who would not allow a man to leave
the stations until he was reinstated, and calling
upon the whole of the police to be united and sup-
port their secretary.
At three stations only—viz., Arolyneux-street
(D), Bow-street (E), and Kensington (T), these
telegrams were read by the delegates to the police,
when they paraded for night duty at 10 o'clock
on Saturday, and nearly the whole declined to go
out on duty. Colonel Labalinondiere was at once
informed, and proceeded to Bow-street station. He
explained to the men the cause of Goodchild being
dismissed, and the whole of the men at once went
on duty. At Molyneux-street and Kensington
the same explanation was given, and in these cases
also the whole of the men marched out, with one
exception—that of Police-constable Brown (T),
who was suspended, and afterwards charged before
a magistrate. •
On Tuesday, Constable Brown, of thelT division,
who declined to go on duty at Kensington, was
charged at the Hammersmith Police-court with
having withdrawn himself from the service of the
force without notice. As, however, the defen-
dant's counsel was unable to attend, the proceed-
ings were adjourned. A summons was granted
against the man for the alleged offence, and he
was liberated on bail.
It is stated that, in accordance with instructions
from Scotland-yard, 180 policemen who refused
to go on duty at the Bow-street station on Satur-
day evening have been suspended from their posi-
tions in the force. Proceedings have been taken
against four men who are charged with absolutely
inciting the mon to desert their duty. The eases
of the remainder have been investigated by the
Commissioner ,and they will remain under sus-
pension.

A sharp punishment has fallen upon the insub-
ordinate policemen who last Saturday refused to
obey the orders of their superiors at three of the
London stations. These men, in all 179, had been
already, as above mentioned, suspended from duty,
and on Wednesday night ordbrs were issued by
Colonel Henderson, after consultation with the
Home Office, dismissing 70 of the Bow-street
policemen out of the 71, and 39 of the Kensington
men out of the 43. The men at Marylebone,
who when appealed to by the Superintendent wont
on duty, have been met by degradation of rank.
At Bow-street Police Station on Wednesday
night a little after 19 o'clock the suspended men
were paraded and the orders read out by the
District Superintendent. The men appeared some-
what surprised, and for a time were dumf bounded.
Before the first surprise:was over, and in the midst
of deep silence, as if the men were .lookimg at all
points of the decision, a man who stood near the
door cried out, "Well, now, we're all dismissed,
and I hope before a year is over our heads the four
District Superintendents will follow us." He then
darted through the door and disappeared, having,
it appeared from the conversation of his comrades,
a wholesome dread of being "run in" on a charge
of being disorderly in the station.
The men then slowly and reluctantly left the
station. Some wanted their money at once, and
were inclined to be insolent when outside; others
preserved their respectful demeanour throughout;
some were moody, while others seemed glad to be
free.

Many of ,the dismissed men have been in the
force from twenty to twenty-five years, and would
have been entitled to a pension; and their past
good conduct has elicited some sympathy on their
behalf.

articles.title: TUE AGRICULTURAL LABOUR
articles.text:
TUE AGRICULTURAL LABOUR

QUESTION.

Mr. Cowper Temple, Member for South Hants,
spoke at Romsey on Wednesday on the agricul-
tural labourers' queation. He argued that the
principle of trade unions could not be applied to
agricultural labour. As a means of improving the
labourers' condition, ho advised giving them a
direct interest in their occupation by the adoption
of piece work, and payment by results, as well as
by awarding premiums for extra produce and extra
stock above the average.

articles.title: CIVIL SERVICE CLERKS AND WRITERS' ASSOCIATION.
articles.text:
CIVIL SERVICE CLERKS AND
WRITERS' ASSOCIATION.

On Monday evening a meeting of Government
writers and their friends was held at the Westmin-
ster Palace Hotel, for the establishment of a
mutual aid and provident institute and widow and
orphans' fund for the junior grades of public
servants. The meeting was largely attended. Mr.
Otway, M.P., occupied the chair, who sajd that
they were all aware of the object which brought
them together. It was a laudabh one, and parti-
cularly so in the case of those who had no
permanent employment. The physicians and other
professions had made provision for their members.
The labouring classes even were in the habit of
'making provision for days of sickness and for the
support of their families. The Civil Service writers
and temporary clerks wore in a position between
these two elassess. The advantage of such an
institution must be patent to all. (Hear, hear.)
Mr. G. Brant moved the following resolution:
That this meeting of "so-called" Civil Service
writers and temporary clerks, having regard to the
fact that no provision is at present made for
granting superannuation to the non-established
employs of the Crown, recognizes the necessity
for the establishment of a provident association,
which shall afford help to its members when aged
and infirm, and provision for their widows and
orphans.
He said that they had been threatened with an
amendment, but he was glad to say that the amend.
merit would not be pressed, so that they would
now go forward as an united body.
Mr. Absolom seconded the resolution, which was
carried unanimously.

Mr. Lodge moved the appointment of a com-
mittee to carry out the foregoing resolution.

The ressolution having been seconded,

Mr. Charley, M.P., supported it, and said that
they could not have confided their interests to
better hands than those of Mr. Otway. (Loud
cheers.)
The motion was carried, as was a motion giving
the thanks of tho meeting to the chairman and
those members of the House of Commons who had
so kindly supported him on this question.

articles.title: BIRMINGHAM JOINERS.
articles.text:
THE BIRMINGHAM JOINERS.

On Thursday Mr. Rupert Kettle gave his
decision in the matter in dispute between the
carpenters and joiners of Birmingham and their
employers. Ho rules that it is quite optional with
any employer whether he provide artificial light
in the winter months, so that his workmen can
commence work before seven o'clock in the morn-
iag. If any master does provide any artificial
light he must pay his outdoor workmen the same
wages as the indoor men, although they may not
be able to work such long hours. In all oases
where the master does not choose to provide artifi-
cial light, the working day for the period between
six weeks before and six weeks after Christmas
should commence at seven a.m. and terminate at
five p.m.

articles.title: BEA.DFORD PLASTERERS'
articles.text:
THE BEA.DFORD PLASTERERS'

LABOUR ER S .

A dispute of three weeks' standing has existed
between those men and their employers. All the
union men were discharged, and other labourers
have been obtained to supply their places. The
dispute is not about time or wages, but with
respect to *lodging money paid to labourers
casually engaged, and who do not reside per-
manently in Bradford. Labourers who have
residences in Bradford are paid lodging money
when called upon to work in distant places. The
employers have secured sufficient men to serve
their purposes, but a few of the union men who
have not obtained work persist in looking after the
strangers and decoying them away from Bradford.
The consequence is that the men cannot be kept at
the jobs, and some heavy works that ought to be
proceeded with, such as the new Town Hall, the
Yorkshire Banking Company's new premises, and
other contracts, are considerably retarded. The
employers have applied to the Chief Constable
to see whether the union Patrols cannot be dealt
with in some way to prevent them from inter-
fering with the men who are at work.

articles.title: FUSTIAN CUTTERS.
articles.text:
THE FUSTIAN CUTTERS.

On Wednesday morning about 300 operatives in
the employ of 141 r. Robert Sheppard, fustian cutter,
Royton and Crompton, near Oldham, left their
work on strike. Operative fustian cutters em-
ployed by other firms are also on strike. The
masters, in consoquence of the present depressed
condition of the trade, had given notice to the
operatives of their intention ta reduce the rate of
wages by from 15 per cent. to 25 per cent. Rather
than submit to the reduction, the operatives have
come out on strike.

articles.title: GENERAL UNION OF
articles.text:
THE GENERAL UNION OF

CARPENTERS.

The forty-eighth annual report of this society
has just been issued, and after referring to the
general adrancement of trades unionism, the
general secretary, Mr. Robert Last, in the report
says :

"A glance at the tables attached to this report
demonstrates that the total number of members is
now 8,686, showing an increase over last year ( f
1,251. Thb total number of lodges is 130, show-
ing an increase of four. New branches have been
opened in Redditcb, Lytham, From°, Banbury,
Guildford, and Aberavon, and the nucleus of a
lodge has been formed in the United States. On
the other hand, the lodge at Mumbles has been
withdrawn, and the following lodges have amal-
gamated :—Newton Heath with Manchester, and
Rochdale Hand-in-hand with Rochdale No. 1.
The total income has been £0,887 19s. 6id., while
the total outlay has been £7,087 ss. lid., the
balance in the hands of the lodges and executive
being £3,761 17s. 60.
"Of this expenditure there has been appro-
priated to members out of work £1,325 is. 10d.;
a substantial alleviation of that most terrible
anxiety in a working man's household, the thought
of how to provide for to-morrow. When it is re-
membered how much the spirits are depressed, and
the best energies broken down by the uncertainty
of being able much longer to keep the wolf from
the door, this portion of our benefit will seem a
sufficient compensation for the duties and respon-
sibilities of membership.
"The Sick and Superannuation Benefit has ab-
sorbed £2,349 17s. bd.; and with regard to this,
the remarks just made apply with double force.
The man who has neglected to insure himself
against the "ills that flesh is heir to "—sickness
and old age—has ever a black shadow before 'him,
He cannot tread the earth as independently as
other men; for he knows that however superior
he may be to tho'frowns of the world at present,
there may come a time when distress, and possibly
beggary will overtake him, The consciousness of
having performed this duty, and the knowledge
that his insurance is (humanly speaking) safe, be-
cause invested in a sound and prosperous concern,
in which he has his due share of representation,
must be fruitful of solace to every thinking man.
"For Tool Benefit we have expended £9l 6s.
sp., a productive outlay, since it restores the
means of livelihood to those who have been tem-
porarily deprived of them.
_ _ .

_ _
"Officers' salaries and general working expenses
have absorbed—the first £962 7s. lid., and the
second, as detailed in the report, £832 18s. lOid.

"The strike benefit has amounted to £697 12s.
4d.; a small sum compared with the extent of
our operations, and a fact that speaks volumes
against the calumny that the object of such asso-
ciations as ours is to foment disputes.
"On account of members deceased (to the num-
ber of forty-ono) we have paid £llO, and on
account of members' deceased wives (forty-seven)
£lBB. These sums, it need scarcely be suid, re-
present the alleviation of an incalculable amount
of family trouble; and the greatest of all earthly
ills has thereby been rendered loss hard to bear.
Pour accidents have absorbed £200."

articles.title: BELFAST BUILDERS.
articles.text:
THE BELFAST BUILDERS.

On Saturday evening a meeting of the Trades
Council at Belfast was held in reference to the
strike which is going on between the Master
Builders' Association and their workmen. The
council consisted of deputies from the various
trades in Belfast, and, as stated by the secretary
at the meeting, represented some fourteen thou-
sand artisans. The grievances of the workmen
having been fully discussed, it was agreed that an
effort should be made towards the settlement of the
dispute between tho stonecutters and their em-
ployers, as it appeared that the carpenters and
joiners had already taken steps towards the
adjustment of their own difficulty.

articles.title: DLACKBURN` CARDROOM
articles.text:
THE DLACKBURN` CARDROOM

HANDS.

A dispute 'in which the] associated cardroom
bands of Blackburn and the district took an active
part, and which 33Idistlicts shad :pledged them-
selves to take united action upon, was brought to
a termination on Monday, A deputation, ap-
pointed at a wages conference held the previous
day, waited upon Messrs, Lewis Brothers, Stanley.
street Mill, and, after an amicable interview, the
claims of the cardroom hands were in the main
conceded, and the expected strike and lock-out was
averted. Messrs. Jackson's weavers have returned
to work,

articles.title: 13IIMINGHAM TIN-PLATE WORKERS.
articles.text:
THE 13IIMINGHAM TIN-PLATE
WORKERS.

On Monday evening a meeting of the operative
tin-plate workers was held at the Public Office,
Moor-street, Birmingham, to receive the report of
the deputation appointed on the 7th inst. to meet
the masters in conference respecting an advonce of
wages. Mr. Davison presided. There was a large
attendance.

The Secretary (Air. Evans) read a report of tho
meeting between the masters and men which
showed that on the suggestion of a master, the
following resolution was passed
That, in our, opinion, you must have Wolver-
hampton working with you in this movement.
We are prepared to aocept any book of prices that
may be agreed upon by the employers 4nd work-
men of the two towns. If Wolverhampton fails
to obtain any advance, we arc willing to pay the
present Wolverhatnpton prices.
He also road a letter from the secretary of the
Wolverhampton Society, stating that the corn.
mittee of the society felt that they were not in a
position to recommend. the members to ask for an
advance at the present time. They felt that
if they were to move now, especially after a state-
ment which had appeared in the newspapers to
the effect that the workmen in Wolverhampton
were paid 9} per cent. more than the men of Bir-
mingham, they Would be unsuccessful.

The Chairman said it was for them to consider
what their next step should he.

Mr. Lewis moved--

That the present price-book ho revised on a
scale of 16 per cent., and articles not ‘t present
in the book be added, and during the revision
that 10 per cont. be paid on the present prices.
Mr. Edwards seconded tho motion.

Mr. Lowe proposed as an amendment—.
That a bonus of 10 per cent. on the present
prices be asked for.
The amendment was seconded by Mr. Watson.
Mr. Evans thought it would be better to have
the book of prices revised.

The amendment was carried.
A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the

businoes.

articles.title: STRIKE OF FARM LABOURERS IN BEDFORDSHIRE.
articles.text:
STRIKE OF FARM LABOURERS IN
BEDFORDSHIRE.

The agricultural labourers in the district of
Southoe, Bedfordshire, have struck for an increase
wages. On Monday night a large meeting, com-
posed of upwards of 1,00.0 labourers, assembled
from different parts of the country, was held at
Southoe. Mr. Bailey, a labouring man from
Offord, was voted to the chair, and strongly urged
his fellow-labourers to be sober-minded throughout
the struggle, and victory was sure. Addresses
were delivered by the founder of the Bedfordshire
Union, and others, and a committee was formed
for the purpose of obtaining subscriptions and
managing matters during the strike.

articles.title: BOILER MAKERS AND IRON SHIP BUILDERS.
articles.text:
THE BOILER MAKERS AND IRON
SHIP BUILDERS.

In the quarterly report of this society for No.
vembor Mr. R. Knight, the secretary, says
We are sorry to see the amount paid for dia.
putes this quarter has increased. Although we
have not paid a largo sum, yet we should be glad
to see our books without such an entry on them,
but
,we suppose that will not be while human
nature remains what it is, and wo rather fear the
amount will increase this present quarter, as some
of the employers appe.ir to take advantage of the
winter months with the short hours, and are in-
clined to put the "screw on." We would, there-
fore, recommend our members not to act too
hastily; use moderation. But while we give you
this advice, we are determined to resist any undue
advantage taken by any employer.
We are well pleased with the increased number
of lodges, the addition to our ranks, and the
goodly sum of money added, to our accumulated
capital. _ _

Three lodges have been opened during the past,
quarter with every prospect of success, waking a
total of 122.

Our members have increased by 874, the largest
number over initiated in the same space of time
since the formation of the society, making a total
on the 30th September of eleven thousand and
forty; this is also the largest number ever on our
books since the society's existence.
. The increme to our fonds is equally gratifying,
as the accumulated capital shown by the returns
amounts to the stun of £21,553 Os. se., and,
taking the balance of the Gainaborough and Dun-
dee lodges at £lO5, will make a total of £21,658
Os. 6111., an increase on the quarter of £2,7/6
16s. lid. We would not boast of our money, but
those who are the best prepared for war have the
surest guarantee of peace. Let our motto be,
"Defence, not defiance."

THE LONDON CABINETMAKERS.

On Thursday evening a delegate meeting of this
trade was held at the Paul's Head Tavern, Paul-

otreet, Finsbury, relative to the 10 per cent. move-
ment.

• Mr. Harry Ham occupied the chair.
The Chairman asked if anyone was aware of
anyone who had paid into the movement who had
not got the 10 per cent. No answer was made.
After some discussion relative to the prices paid
by different shops, the Secretary stated that the
proportion of society men who had continued to
pay to the movement was one-half, and that of
the non-society men one-fourth.

Mr. Murphy said he believed that some men
were prepared to fall back on the movement, and
it was unfair to close it at present. He thought
the accounts should be ,balanced, and that the
question of closing the movement should be con-
sidered at the end of the month.

The Chairman said that in respectable shops in
the East End the advances of 10 per cent. had
been retained.

After it had been proposed that the closing of
the movement :should be considered at the end of
the present month; that it should continue till the
first week in March; and that it should cease at
the end of the present month, the following
resolutions were proposed and carried.
1. That the delegate meetings should cease at
the end of the present month.
2. That the account of £l4 odd due from this
movement to the Alliance Cabinetmakers' Asso-
ciation should be paid at once.
3. That the accounts be balanced up to Nov.
23rd, and audited.
4. That two auditors be appointed.
6. That at the: termination of the subscriptions
the funds in hand be invested in the Alliance
Cabinetmakers' Association, in trust for this move-
ment. _ _

6. That the present delegate committee, with a
chairman and secretary, be appointed to watch
over the interests of the 10 per cent. movement,
with power, when any employer attempts to take
off the percentage, t, rail a delegate meeting, and
take such steps as may be necessary for the benefit
of this movement, and that they shall receive no
remuneration for their services, except when called
away from their employment.
The secretary declared a balance in band of
£33 lii, ad.

After a vote of thankslto the chairman, the pro-
ceedings were closed.

articles.title: LONDON WHEELWRIGHTS AND SMITHS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON WHEELWRIGHTS
AND SMITHS.

On Saturday evening the above united trades
held a crowded and general meeting at the
Foresters' Hall, Wilderness-row, to hear a me-
morial read, which is to be presented to their
employers, requesting a reduction of the hours of
labour to 64 hours a week, and an advance of 10
percent. on piece-work.

- gr. Gaywo-od occupied the chair, who said there
were 700 members in the league. They intended
to go before their employers in a respectful man-
mart and they wanted their support. They had
drawn up a memorial which would be rend.
The secretary read the memorial, which was
accepted by the meeting.
Mr. Dwight said he thought the memorial fair,
both as regards employers and employed, and
should anything not meet with their approbation,
he hoped they would give their employers no
grounds for complaints.
Ho proposed that the memorial, as now read, be
adopted and forwarded to their employers on the
2nd'of December.

The resolution was seconded by Mr. Tompkins,
and carried nnanimouoly.

articles.title: CLYDE ENGINEERS' DISPUTE.
articles.text:
THE CLYDE ENGINEERS' DIS-
PUTE.

A conference between the representatives
of the Clyde shipbuilders and the Engineers'
Association and the Iron Trades Short Time
League was held in Glasgow on Tuesday for the
purpose of discussing the questions in dispute bo-
tween them as to hours and wages. It may be
explained that the men have been locked out since
Friday last, and that the masters suggested a con-
ference. A similar conference was held in Feb-
ruary last, when it was understood by the men to
have been agreed that the men should get, on the
Ist of March last, the 54 hours, instead of the 67,
without a reduction of wages; and that from the
Ist November they were to work 51 hours without
a reduction of wages. The masters in their con-
ference on Tuesday intimated their willingness to
give the 61 hours, to be divided into such periods
each day as the men should choose, and to submit
the question as to the exact meaning of the agree-
ment in February Met to arbitration. The dele-
gates from the men replied that they had no
autliordy to comply with such a request, but added
that they would submit the proposal to a meeting
of the men to be held.

articles.title: LONDON POSTMEN.
articles.text:
THE LONDON POSTMEN.

At an early hour on Tuesday morning the
inspector on duty at the branch Post-office,
Buckingham Palace-gate, called the, letter-carriers
and sorters for the south-western district, number-
ing over 100, together, and informed them that he
had a communication from the Postmaster-General
to read to them respecting the " stripes " that had
been awarded to about twenty-five of their
number for meritorious conduct. The men, how-
ever, with one or two exceptions, vociferously
called out, "We don't want to hear it; put it down,
Sir." "We won't hear another word." "We
want more wages, not stripes or Mr. Monsell's
buttons." "It will disgrace us to wear stripes,
and we shall be laughed and jeered through the
streets. Buttons and stripes won't feed our
children. It's all favouritism." The inspector
begged the men to listen, and made another
attempt to read the report, but the:uproar now
became greater still. Yells, hooting, groans,
whistling, and other discordant noises were kept
up until the inspector had to return without
reading Mr. Monsell's report.
This being reported to the head-office, another
document was brought forward on Wednesday
morning acquainting the men that if they did not
choose to accept the stripes they had better send
In their resignations. The other branch offices are
equally averse from the stripes.
A great meeting of the whole of the carriers is
to be called immediately by the delegates from
each branch office.

articles.title: LOCK-OUT IN THE STAFFORDSHIRE POTTERIES.
articles.text:
THE LOCK-OUT IN THE STAFFORD-
SHIRE POTTERIES.

The lock-out, involving the idleness of thirty-
five thousand men, has come to an end. A con-
ference of representative masters and men was
held on Tuesday afternoon, and the question of
"good from hand" veraus "good from oven"
being left to Mr. Davenport, referee of the Board
of Arbitration, be decided that it could not be
arbitrated upon. It was then withdrawn by the
men, and, an understanding being come to to refer
all wages questions to the Board of Arbitration,
the lock-out was declared by the masters to be at
an end. Work will therefore be resumed at
once.

articles.title: WOLVERHAMPTON IRONWORKERS.
articles.text:
THE WOLVERHAMPTON IRON-
WORKERS.

An important meeting of ironmasters was held
on Wednesday; Mr. G. G. Darker presiding; to
take into consideration the whole subject of iron-
workers' wages. After a long discussion it was
resolved that the chairman should communicate
with the chairman of the Coalmastera' Associa-
tion stating the opinion of the meeting that the
time had come when it was desirable to consider
the whole subject of colliers' wages, their hours of
labour, and the prices of coal, and asking advice as
to the calling of a general meeting of members as
early as possible.

articles.title: TEE SOME RSE TSH RE LAB OURERS.
articles.text:
TEE SOME RSE TSH RE LAB OURERS.

On Monday evening a meeting of the Agricul-
tural Labourers took place at Stoke St. Mary,
Somerset, to consider the prospeots2,of, forming a
Union in that district,

Mr. Burt was elected chairman, who 'offered a
few remarks on the subject of the meeting.

Mr. G. C. Strawbridge, from Taunton, addressed
the meeting, and the following resolution was
passed :

That this meeting is of 'opinion that a Branch
of the Agricultural Labourers' Union ought to be
formed in this district for the purpose of improv-
ing their present condition.

-1
Mr. R. Trump seconded the resolution, which
was carried with a few dissents.

articles.title: BIRKINGHAINI METAL TRADE.
articles.text:
THE BIRKINGHAINI METAL TRADE.

A meeting of employers in the metal rolling,
brass tube, and bedstead trades was held at the
Birmingham Exchange, on Wednesday, to con-
sider the notices of strike, of which there was
nearly a thousand, given in last week to enforce
the demand of the men for an advance of 16 per
Cent. in wages. It was unanimously resolved to
resist the demand to the utmost, and in the event
of a partial strike to support any firms which
might be singled out for experiment. Such of the
men as may think proper to withdraw their
notices before the strike will be allowed to retain

not to re-engage any who may join in the strike.
This virtually amounts to a lock-out.

articles.title: NOTTINGHAM ORGANIZED TRADES ASSOCIATION.
articles.text:
NOTTINGHAM ORGANIZED
TRADES ASSOCIATION.

The monthly meeting of the Nottingham
Organized Trades Association was held at the Sir
F. Burdett Inn, Mount-street, on Wednesday
evening, when representatives from 15 societies
were present; Mr. French was in the chair.
The Secretary reported the result of a visit by a
deputation appointed by the Council of the Associa-
tion to a large firm in the dyeing trade, between
whom and their workmen a dispute had existed
for several weeks, the effect of the interview being
the arrangement of terms satisfactory to both
parties, whereby the men resumed their employ-
ment. Much pleasure was evinced by the Council
with the manner the deputation were received; an
opinion also prevailing that had such a course
been adopted at the outset an open rupture would
either have been• avoided altogether or at least
existed a very brief time.
The Council, at its previous meeting,:having
decided to call a number of the leading members
of trade societies together to meet the Rev. H.
Solly, of London, who desired to bring before
them the adyisability of establishing a trades club
and hall for Nottingham, a report of the proceed-
ings was supplied by those who were present and
the following resolution was adopted :
That this Council, having heard a report from
members who attended the meeting at the
Mechanics' Institution to hear a statement from
Mr. Solly on trades clubs and halls, fully approves
of the object, and will use its influence in pro-
moting the formation of a trades dub and hall for
Nottingham, and urges the desirability of trades
societies using their utmost endeavours to bring
about a speedy realization of the purpose contem-
plated.
The programme of the business to be discussed
by the Trades' Union Congress at Leeds, in
January next, was considered, and it was unani-
mously resolved that Messrs. D. Higham and W.
flicking be chosen to represent the association.

articles.title: LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.
articles.text:
LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.

On Wednesday, at the weekly meeting of
the London School Board, Lord Lawrence,
who presided, said that he had been requested
by the Rev. Canon Miller to read to the Board
a letter which that rev, gentleman had re-
ceived from the Education Department, stat-
ing that they were perfectly satisfied with
the explanation he had given respecting the
alleged expulsion of a child from a school in
Greenwich, on account of her attending a
Methodist Suqday School.
The Rev. Mr. Waugh complained that the
Education. Department had decided the
matter without giving a hearing to the parents
of the child or himself.
Mr. Freeman referred to the balance-sheet
which he laid before the Board at the last
meeting, and invited criticism upon it.
The Rev. Canon Cromwell remarked that
Mr. Freeman stated last week the Board had
been spending during the past six months
only what a halfpenny in the pound would
cover. He (the Rev. Mr. Cromwell) found
that the expenses during that time had been
£77,000. This represented something more
like a penny in the pound. He also found
that there were 26,000 children on the books
of the Board schools. Taking 20,000 as an
average attendance, each child paid only lid.
a week school fees. If that were so, the Board
had carried out a more general remission of
fees than had been sanctioned, and without
havingeascertained whether the parents were
or were not able to pay. The education of each
of these children could not cost less than 4d.
or sd. a week.

Mr. Freeman explained that to do what
the Rev. Mr. Cromwell desired, an application
to the Local Government Board would be
necessary. There were books at the Board
office, which gave the information. It was
quite true that the Board had been spending
during the past six months only • a halfpenny
rate. The error into which the rev, gentle-
man had fallen was that he had included in
the current expenses what would be taken
out of a loan extending over fifty years.
After disposing of the business on the paper,
which was principally of a routine character,
the Board adjourned.

articles.text:
LIBOUR-SAVING MA_CIIINERY.

On Thursday the Minister of Japan, with
members of his suite, together with American
and English employers of labour, visited the
works of Messrs. Allan, Ransome, and Co., in
King's-road, Chelsea, to view some newly-
invented labour-saving machinery of remark-
able construction and power. The strikes of
workmen in the building trades, the increased
cost of production in the carpentry and joinery
branches of those trades, and the diflioulties
caused to employers by the restrictions
.of
Trades Unions, have each had their share in
directing the attention of engineers to find
the means of meeting the pressure caused by
. the contracted amount of available skilled
labour; and the machines exhibited on Thurs-
day were in every way so perfect that it is not
easy to see how hand labour will hold its own.
The first machine inspected was a portable
saw frame. Any one who has seen the old
saw-pits, where the " top sawyer" and the
"bottom sawyer" laboured from morninif to
night and day after day in cutting a log int?
planks, would be greatly astonished to see this
comparatively small machine, attended only
by one man, cut up the body of a huge oak
into 14 planks at once, it having 12 saws,
which cut through the whole bulk of wet wood
in something less than half an hour. A
mortising machine, the invention of Mr.
Richards, of Philadelphia, was set to work, and
accurately and cleanly cut in a few moments
mortises which would have taken a workman
hours. A moulding machine, for cutting
mouldings, did in a minute 35 feet of work,
which would have taken a skilled workman
many hours, and this work could apparently
be done by a boy. In what was called a
" general joining machine" there was apparently
no limit to the work to be done, the one
machine cutting mortises, shaping blocks,
planking, carving out banisters, and turning
in a few minutes a plain block of wood into a
perfectly carved piece of work. Another
machine, exceedingly small and unpretentious,
was shown to be capable of planing any sort
of work, oval or flat, and at the same time a
revolving chisel cut mortises with celerity and
accuracy. A very fine piece of machinery p
one which outs raised or recessed panelst in
other words, which can cut the sunk or raised
ornamental work in wood now so highly prized
and so dearly paid for, as the best and most
skilled work. By another machine, an American
invention, but improved by the Moss?.
Ransome, a door can be finished—that is,
cleanly sand•papered on both sides—in three
minutes. The planing and trying-up of work,
or what would be properly called the
" trueing"-up, by which is meant the nice
work of making blocks of wood exactly likt?
one another, in order to be put together" true,"
work which is done with an infinite deal of
hand labour, is, by one of Ransome's machines,
done at once and perfectly in a few minutesl
all the blocks, of whatever size, being placed
together and turned out as like as peas, and
mathematically correct in every respect. A
band saw machine, by which both fine and
rough work was cut in all sorts of shapes, and
a saw cutting machine, with F. Ransome's
patent stone, were among the other works
shown. With one or two of these machines
an employer, with a man and a boy as staff,
could turn out as much work as 20 or 30 men,
and never be troubled about the nine hours,
eight hours, or any other movement. The
remarkable fact about these machines is that
they are not limited to the pattern, shape, or
character of wood, for the knives are changed
in a few minutes, end, whatever the class of
work required, it can be done at once. The
inspection lasted for several hours, and all the
visitors expressed themselves delighted with
these new machines, some of which are to go
to the Vienna Exhibition.

articles.text:
CORRgSPONDENCE.

We are not answerable for the opinions expressed by our
correspondents. All communications must be addressed
to the Editor of the Bel-litrs. Those who desire their
letters to appear should write as briefly as possible, as
: our space is so limited, and on one side of the pap or
only.

UPROARIOUS AGRICULTURAL
MEETING.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
8114-Will you allow me to report through
your widely-circulated journal the proceedings
of a meeting at Langtoft, Spalding, I had
the honour of addressing last week. Accord-
ing to bill, I took my stand near an inn and
commenced my lecture (or address), hoping
that no prejudice existed in the village to any
great extent; but before I had proceeded far
with my remarks, I found that some of the
Billingsgate collegians were present, and how
to account for the foul language that was
uttered by those frantic creatures, I fail to
know. One of the farmers, not being disposed
to work himself, offered 5 half- o rowns to any man
who would pull me out of the chair and put
me into the water to cool my parched tongue.
But to cut the report short, farmers, bakers,
engine-drivers, and others of a similar class
were exceedingly anxious to lay rough hands
Upon me. I may here say, that many thanks
are due to the police officer, who did his best to
prevent a collision. But so determined were
those aristocrats to give me a dose of mixture,
that a collision did take place before the
meeting ended; atid in consequence of the
glass windows and the gentlemen's broad
cloth being rather tender, they gave way
during the struggle; but on account of the
prepondering number of democrats, I was soon
brought out of bondage, and I feel more than
ever convinced of this fad, that it is the
employer and not the employed that are
agitated by the remarks made from time to
time by the so-called public agitators. I
would ask, Mr. Editor, what has education
done for those men? Has it made them what
they assume to be in their social circle? No;
far from it—for their words are base, their
actions a disgrace, and their general deport-
ment a blank contradiction of their profession,
viz., we are gentlemen. I hope, sir, the
children of the industrial classes will receive
an education that contains the elements of
humanity, charity, temperance, &0., &o.
Yours truly, AN OrtGANISER.
Spalding.

r DE QUIBUSDAM REBUS.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

adopt- this heading because it is to ,
two very unlike subjects that I wish to draw '
attention.
The first is—l have observed that 300
agricultural labourers are about to proceed
from Plymouth to Queensland, in Australia.
I hope the poor fellows before taking this, to
them, all important step, have been satisfied
by persons on whom they can safely, depend,
that the climate of Queensland is such, that
they will be able to earn their bread there
without danger to life. Queensland is close
on the tropics, and its products are sugar and

and I hope that, in order to procure it, they
have not employed that class of persons, who
at one time repruited for the British army,

am afraid that in this matter of emigration,
Intending emigrants should put no faith in
any evidence except that of their brethren who
have preceded them.
• The other subject I wish to bring to notice
is the cost of retrenchment. Some member
of Parliament should call for a list of all
pensions (whether since commuted or not)
granted during the last ten years, in oon-
sequence of bankruptcy and other law court
reforms, and of retrenchments in the civil
and military services of the country generally,
in fact, in all the Government departments;
giving the names of the recipients, and dis-
tinguishing such pensions from those granted
for long service. In most cases, the men so
pensioned after short service, should have
been forced to accept re-employment in
analogous offices.

articles.title: November 12th, 1872.
articles.text:
November 12th, 1872.

THE TRADES UNIONS CONGRESS.
To the Editor of the BEE-lime.
_

Sin,—As the time approaches for the hold-
ing of tile annual Trades Congress, the minds
of some become more directly interested and
anxious, though, to some extent, tampered
with glowing anticipations as to the results of
its deliberations upon some of the most itnpor-
tant matters taken into consideration by it, or
similarly constituted assemblies. Pre-eminence
being accorded to the discussion of the
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1871, its in-
fluence and effect upon our great organizations
during the time it has been in operation—to
consider the report of, and to pass judgment
upero, the way the Parliamentary Committee
have endeavoured to grapple with the question
(not omitting, I hope, to thank Messrs. Harri-
son, Walton, and Bosley for their timely and

commendatory letters on the subject) ; also to
decide whether the action of that Committee
shall be endorsed and repeated by its suc-
cessors during the next session of Parliament.
I feel quite sure it will be readily admitted
that the Parliamentary Committee have done
that which they have with a singleness of pur-
pose and desire to alleviate as speedily as
possible the injustice experienced by the trades
unionists in various parts of the country.
This they are entitled to; but it would be un-
wise for us to let respect for individuals con-
trol our judgment as to our future poliey.
We can, and should, thank Mr. Vernon Har-
court kindly and sincerely for past favours,
but inasmuch after doing my best to read,
mark, learn, and inwardly digest his com-
munication which appeared in the BEE-HIVE,
I can only conclude that be is totally opposed
to the decision of the last Trades Congress, as
embodied in resolution, and is prepared to
urge the necessity of gagging the mouths and
restricting the liberties and privileges of that
portion of the community calling themselves
trades unionists. We are bound, in honour and
justice to ourselves, to bid him a very quick
Good day, Sir.' I fear that those who
supported this bill failed in comprehending
the detrimental influences consequent of their
so doing. To amend an Act of Parliament is
to admit the principle of it. When, and
where' did any body of unionists express ap-
proval of the principles of the 1871 Act?
never heard of any. The principle of right
and justice to us is involved in it, and playing
see-saw with that principle is a reprehensible
proceeding, and one that is calculated to recoil
upon our interests. The Committee asked for
amendment, we want total repeal; we have
got neither. I readily admit that in the ab-
sence of total repeal amendment is desirable,
providing it were a real one, and could be ob-
tained without us compromising our rights.
Had it not have been for the incessant demand
for manhood suffrage, I do not think trades
unionists would have that electoral power they
now have. The demand was for the .reoogni-
tion of a great principle. Amendment, in the
shape of a compromise, was readily offered,
and so I think it might have been with us
in this instance. By strictly and rigidly adher-
ing to our rights we may effect an improve-
ment, if not the consumation of our aspira-
tions. Neither do we know what I think it is
important we should, and that by a division
in the House, what members are in favour of
a total repeal? Are there any? If so, let us
know their names and the constituencies they
represent, and if there are positively none at
all, let us know it for our future guidance.
The late division upon Mr. Harcourt's Bill is
no criterion whatever; there are those besides
himself which supported that but would op-
pose total repeal.
_ _ _

The association I have the pleasure of be-
longing to has resolved, in addition to send-
ing a delegate to the Congress, to urge these
or similar views, to take upon themselves the
responsibility of introducing to the next
session of Parliament a Bill to effect (if passed)
the total repeal of the '7l Act, and. it would
materially assist us in so doing to have the
support and the approval of the Congress, and
the hearty co-operation of unionists in general.
I beg most respectfully to submit this for their
careful attention and consideration. Should
the Congress decide that the Bill of last
session be re-introduced, T fear we shall feel
ourselves constrained to oppose that decision
by persevering in our course alone and single-
handed, a by no means desirable eventuality,
and one which, I hope, the good sense of the
delegates to the Congress will avert by being
faithful to that expressed public opinion when
and wherever they have had an opportunity of
meeting together to take it into consideration.
Hoping, Sir, you will be able to obligti by in-
serting this in your paper as early as con-
venient, I remain, Sir,yours truly,
ALFRED THORNTON',

Secretary of the
.Nottingham Trades Union

Association.
49, Truman-street.

articles.title: MONEY MARKET AND THE BANK
articles.text:
THE MONEY MARKET AND THE BANK

OF ENGLAND.

To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

Sru,—Under the above title an anonymous
correspondent, signing himself "IL U. W.,"
has addressed a letter to your contemporary,
the Daily News, above two columns in length,
and it would be difficult to bring forward a
stronger example of the great superiority of
the french mode—and so successfully adopted
by yourself—of not inserting anonymous com-
munications. The editor is in a different
position, for his leading articles are valued
more or less as the public) believe in his
honesty and sagacity.
This anonymous letter may have been
written by the Governor of the Bank of Eng-
land. Then the public would have sagacity
but be cheated out of that honesty, which con-
sists in a writer being disinterested. Ido not
believe that the Governor of the Bank of
England would have so committed himtelf to
so silly a production as to have signed his
name to 4t, although he may have been well
pleased to have seen one of his parasites obtain
the insertion of such a document in so respect-
able a paper as the Daily News.

For this anonymous correspondent, perceiv-
ing that the feeling against the monopoly of
the Bank of England is increasing in intensity,
and that any fair inquiry is sure to end in its ex-
tinction, has actually the assurance to propose
that the inquiry shoed be a secret one—not
in so many words, for that would be too bad,
and certain to be rejected—but under the pre-
tence that a commission would be a better
mode of inquiry than that by a select com-
mittee of both Houses of Parliament, which
was the mode adopted by Sir Robert Peel
when he wanted a fair public inquiry into the
working of the Bank Act of 1844.
And this anonymous correspondent conceals
the fact that there has already been an inquiry
into the working of the Bank Act of 1844,
and that, too, proposed by the author of the
Bill, the late Sir Robert Peel, who on moving
for the appointment of the committee, can-
didly confessed that the Bill had not answered
the expectations. The Lords reported strongly
against the Bill; the Commons were equally
divided, and, therefore, made no report; and
it was said at the time, that one of the most
important members had been induced not to
attend.

Be this as it may, there stands the nasty
fact, that a majority of the Lords committee
strongly denounced the Bill in 1844, and half
the members of the Commons committee enter-
tained a similar opinion. Ido not know
whether Mr. Gladstone was or not upon that
committee, but if he wile he would certainly
vote with Sir Robert Peel.

Now, the directors of the Bank of England
and their parasites have always been in
favour of the Bank Act of 1844, and are
extremely desirous that there should be no
inquiry, but if there must be one, then that
it should be as little as possible; and, there-
fore, this anonymous correspondent purposes
that it should be considered not by fair and
open committees of both Houses of Parlia-
ment, but by a commission, sitting here one
day, then another, sometimes with closed, at
others, with open doors; in short, make the
inquiry such that the public will have the
greatest difficulty in attending.
There is an abundance of money in the
market if it was regulated solely by the law
of supply and demand; instead of which it is
regulated solely by the directors of the Bank
of England, when monopoly enables' them to
charge the whole of the agricultural, manufac-
turing, commercial, and trading interests of
these realms 7 per cent. discount, instead of
4 per cent.; and Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Lowe
permit the directors to do this, simply because
neither of them understands the subjeot.—l
am, Sir, your very obedient servant,
Rion Y WABOIT.

articles.title: HYDE-PARK MEETINGS.
articles.text:
THE HYDE-PARK MEETINGS.

On Monday morning the adjourned sum-
monses against the participators in the Hyde-
park meeting in favour of the Fenian convicts
on Sunday, the 3rd instant, were appointed to
be heard at the Marlborough-street Police-
court, before Mr. Newton. The names of the
defendants are as foliows :—Messrs. Bailey,
Mooney, Pottle, Murray, Clarke, O'Leary,
Chaddook, M'Donnell, Odger, Butler, and De
Morgan.
Mr. Poland appeared for the Government;
Mr. Baker Greene appeared for Bailey,
Mooney, Pottle, Clarke, and Chaddook ; and
Mr. S. Hallett for O'Leary and Butler.
The case of Bailey was first taken, and
evidence having been gtven tending to show
that the defendant had contravened the
rules made under the Parks Regulation Act,
Mr. Baker Greene addressed the magistrate,
contending that the charge had no founda-
tion; and that there being a right to speak
in the Park according to the Act, the rule pro-
hibiting public meetings was void.
Mr. Newton went over the various rules and
regulations which had been referred to. He
was of opinion that though rules when milde
must be laid before Parliament when sitting,
yet it could never be meant that because Par
liament was not sitting rules should not be
made. Having reviewed the arguments of
both learned counsel, he came to the opinion
that the rules were properly made and enforced
legally. There was an old expression that
those who run may read; and Ito considered
that all who saw the rules must know what
they meant. He thought the defendant
was rightly brought here, not having observed
those rules, and the question now was what
punishment to inflict. After what had been
said by the learned counsel, that he meant to
appeal, although not thinking it a case which
called on him to inflict a severe penalty, he
must inflict such a fine as would enable the
defendant to take the ease to a higher court.
Under these circumstances he should call on
him to pay a fine of £6, or one month's im-
prisonment.
After some conversation it was agreed that
a ease should be stated and taken to a higher
court.

Mr. Hallett wished to make some remarks.
having been summoned under a penal statute,
It was the practice of the learned judges not
to deliver judgment until they had heard, all
the arguments.
Mr. Newton did not intend to hear any
other summonses while an appeal Nos un-

decided, and the rest of the summonses must be
adjourned sine die.
Mr. Hallett considered his clients suffered
great injustice by this arrangement.
Mr. Odger—l must say one word.
Mr. Newton—Officers, please clear the
court.

It was announced by placard that an open-
air meeting would be held at 8 o'clock on
Monday evening in Trafalgar-square, to
hear the result of the prosecutions, and to
protest against the action of the Government
in their endeavour to put down the right of
public meeting and freedom of speech.' Heavy
rain, however, was falling from six till about
nine, and no open-air meeting took place!
The members of the Defence Committee and
the delegates assembled, however, at tho Boar's
Head Tavern, Long-acre, under the presidency
of Mr. W. Osborne. Several of the defendant.
who had appeared at the police-court were
present. Mr. Odger addressed the meeting,
and strongly expressed his dissatisfaction with
the line of defence taken up by Mr. Baker
Greene, counsel for Mr. Bailey, whose case
had just been decided upon by the magistrate.
He complained that Mr. Greene had given up
the chief point of the defence, viz., that the
rules and regulations of the Park were not yet
law, not having been laid upon the table of the
House of Commons or sanctioned by Parlia-
ment. HO believed that the superior court
would be with them on that point if it came
before them, but which it could not do under
the appeal as it now stood. He would, there-
fore, suggest to the Defence Committee that
they should not prosecute the present appeal,
but pay the fine of .£5 and costs. His case
might then be taken, and as he was going to
defend himself, he should rest his case mainly
on the point of law which Mr. Greene had so
unaccountably given up, and if he was con-
victed, let the appeal be made in his case,
which would really test the whole matter.
There was considerable difference of opinion as
to the course to be pursued. Eventually,
however, the matter was referred to the Defence
Committee for their consideration.

Two Liberals and one Conservative returned

a visit to this country, embarked at Woolwich
on her return to Holland.

It is announced from Madrid that, though
the King of Spain is better, the fever and pain
have not yet left him.

Itinerant musicians with concertinas are
often a source of great annoyance to travellers
on the London lines. A man who was in the
habit of torturing people in this way, and of
riding upon the Metropolitan Railway without
paying his fare, was on Monday fined 40s.
by the Marylebohe police magistrate, with the
alternative of a month's imprisonment with

HGeneral Changarnier made his long-pro-
mised attack on M. Gambetta in the National
Assembly on Monday. He not only denounced
the ex-Dictator's speeches as politically and
socially revolutionary, but censured the
Government for permitting them. M. Gam-
betta would not be drawn into a reply. He
left the defence to the Ministry, whieh was at
first not very ably represented by M. Lefranc.

the Tribune twice, and rebutting some per-
sonal remarks Of Changarnier with energy
and dignity, and with the result of modifying
the vote of the Chamber into one expressing
confidence in the Government while condemn-
ing the Grenoble oration.

Along the whole coast of North Germany
from Pillau to Schleswig, a strong north-east
wind was blowing for three days successively,
the tide rising each day higher than the pre-
ceding, till on the 14th, at Stralsund, it was
7 feet 6 inches above the ordinary level. The
distress caused by the inundation is very great,
and an appeal is to be made throughout Ger-
many for assistance.

land and Scotland, and a coMmittee was ap-

to protest against a proposal of the School
Board to spend £BO,OOO upon new schools. It
was alleged by the speakers that the existing
accommodation would suffice for 4,000 children
more, and it was resolved to memorialise the
Government to send down an inspector to in-
quire into the matter.

Bench, applied on behalf of the Tichborne
Claimant, for a rule nisi calling on the Crown
to tillOW cause why, in this important case, a
writ of procedendo should not issue—or, in
