Particulars were received at Hull on Mon-
day from the Vice-Consul at Ronne of the loss
of the steamer Herald, in the Baltic. When
the ship was struck the crew took to the boat,
but were unable to move away from the
steamer's side before she foundered, and
capsized the boat, which, however, soon
lighted, and the greater part of the men had
succeeded in again getting into her, when a
second time she was capsized. Three of the
poor fellows then got upon the keel, but in the
course of the night, two of then) were washed
off, At 'length the fireman, Atherton, was
seen by some fisherman, and picked up
terribly exhausted.

Aberdeen Highlanders.

Mr. }Ebbed, M.P., Secretary to the Local
Government Board, presiding at a conference
held at the rooms of the Social Science Asso-
ciation, in reference to the Poor-law adminis-
tration, was able to congratulate those present

the country, the diminution of vagrancy, and.

co-operation of outside reformers. The prin-
cipal decision arrived at by the conference was

wager, came up on Tuesday for judgment.

papers to be printed in which he declared he

At the Clerkenwell Police-court, on Mon-
day, there were 42 charges of drunkenness;

There is apparently every reason to believe
that the crisis in France will end in the adop-
tion by the Assembly of a vote of confidence
in M. Thiers, which will be adroitly associated
with a proposal for the partial renewal of the
Assembly to the extent of one-fifth—thereby
definitively, though by a compromise_, resolving
the difficulty with regard to its Constituent
power. The President has been visited by
numerous deputies, as well as by the repre-
sentatives of foreign Powers, all expressing
their sympathy with him in the crisis, and the
hope that he will remain at the head of the
State.

a young man, Augustus Elliott, whom the
jury, without leaving the box, found guilty

fortunate girl, with whom he had kept com-
pany, in Northport-street, Hoxton. It may,

land, on Wednesday in reference to the brutal
Murder at Spennymoor on Saturday, when a
man, named Joseph Waine, was dragged out
of his house, and kicked to death before his

fering—because he had declined, to take part

coroner empanelled a jury from a neighbouring
town, and, having formally opened the court,

mortem examination.

haven, from Briton Ferry, with coals,

-

blow across tho face, upon which Sweetman
drew a six-chamber revolver and fired three
shots, all of which missed.- Sweetman was
committed for trial without bail.

Anne Parsons has been charged before the
Worcester magistrates with attempting to
murder her two children. On the 7th inst.,
the prisoner, in a fit of fury after a quarrel
with her husband, threw the children out of
the first-floor window into the yard. They
were both dreadfully injured, one of them
having its thigh broken, and they are still in
the infirmary and in a dangerous state. Pri-
soner was sentenced to two months' bard
labour.

Advices from Varzin state that Prince Bis-
marck has now completely recovered, and has
been able to leave his room.

The Daily Hews New York correspondent,
in writing of the recent Presidential contest
in the United States, says that never before
has an American eleotoral campaign been con-
ducted with so little scruple, or so much money
been spent to influence votes. The Greeley
Committee in New York is said to have ex-
pended about 250,000 dollars. This would
have been a moderate allowance for legitimate
expenses. It is estimated, however, that the
Administration spent from four to five million
dollars. There are 60,000 men in the United
States holding office at the will of the Presi-
dent, and each of these was forced to contri-
bute on an average fifty dollars.

An Edinburgh eattle salesman, named John
Martin, was fined by the Oxford magistrates
£lO and costs for cruelty to cattle. Defendant
had sent ten cows from Kilmarnock to Oxford
—the journey occupying thirty-five hours—
without providing food and water. The ero-
seoution was instituted by the Royal Society
for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals.

The whole of the sixteen Ministers were
present at Monday's Cabinet Council.

The Prince Imperial of Tirane() has joined
the Royal Military Academy Woolwich as
a cadet.

By the death of Mr. Dyee Nicol, M.P., at
the age of 67, the number of vacant seats in
the House of Commons is raised to five—viz.,
Derry, Forfarshire, the Orkneys, Cork City,
and Kincardineshire. The first two are vacant
through the acceptance of office on the pert
of the late members ; and the others through
death. All three of the deceased members
wore Liberals.

An influentially-attended meeting was bold
in Dublin on Monday, at which it was re-
solved to adopt measures for raising a national
memorial to the late Mr. John Francis
Maguire, M.P.

On Monday morning the Countess Clonmel
died at her residence, Bishopscourt, county
Kildare. The immediate cause of death was
bronchitis, but her ladyship had been ailing
for some time.

Edward Hancock, butcher, who murdered
his wife at Priors Hardwick, Warwickshire,
Wednesday week, by stabbing her in the
thigh, was on Monday committed for trial on
the capital charge by the Southern magistrates.
The prisoner was madly jealous of the deceased
without cause. The only additional evidence
was that of their daughter, Elizabeth Hancock,
a child six years of age, who, whilst being put
to bed, saw her father come from an adjoining
room and stab her mother. The little girl
seemed heartbroken whilst giving evidence,
which produced deep emotion in court.

Mr. Morley, M.P., on Tuesday laid the
foundation stone of a new Congregational
church in the midst of the Colleges at Cam-
bridge University. It is to cost X 12,000. The
hon. gentleman promised to add £230, to his
subscription of £3OO, on condition that the
building was opened free from debt.

President Grant's Niessage to the American
Congress in December is expected to give
evidence of a milder and more conciliatory
spirit in Givernment quarters towards the
South, due to the recent electoral vote and the
moderation of the Bouthern press.

The demand everywhere of the artisans employed in
our great centres of industry for direct representation of
labour has developed into such an active life during the
existence of the present Parliament that it has been
deemed advisable by the Labour Representation Lettiplo

plan of united action for the purpose of ensuring the
return to the next Parliament of some, members belonging
to the ranks of Labour.

and consistency during the last four years than hereto-
fore, from the manifest inability of other classes, however
well disposed, either adequately to represent, or speak for
interests they cannot, from want of experience or associa.
tion, understand; while, on the opposite side the persever-
ing interference of Parliament with the customs and
trade associations of artisans, renders imperative' the
serious attention of the working classes to the necessity
of combination for the purpose of directing their power of
franchise in order to secure an entrance for mon of their
own thought, or order, into the House of Commons.

A Committee (as below) was duly apointed to carry

SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 23, 1872.

THE FIREMAN GUERNSEY'S

FUNERAL,

TIIE young fireman who was crushed and
burned to death in the conflagration of the
City Flour Mill, has been buried by the side
of Superintendent BRAIDWOOD and Fireman
FORD, with the high honours of a public)
funeral. Simple, in point of pomp, as were
the funeral obsequies, the long march of such
a procession from the scene of the fire to Abney
Park Cemetery necessarily attracted multitu-
dinous observation, and cannot but have left a
deep impression upon the mind of every
spectator. The silent eloquence of such a
Beene was beyond all spoken eulogy or audible
sermon. The highest and last honours that
the living can bestow are conferred upon
the man who loses his life in the doing of his
duty. The rank and station of the self-
sacrificed make no difference in the account.
Under such circumstances the simple fireman
receives from his contemporaries an equal
recompense with the splendid Field Marshal.
Each died at his post, both in the service of
their generation, neither counting his life dear
unto himself, so that be pursued the course on
which he had entered to the end.
Examples of this stedfastness and devotion
„ are doubtless more numerous than is super&
cially supposed. Yet, as publicity is, with
most of us, necessary in order to impression,
we ought the more carefully to note those
instances of death in duty which transpire

to the general knowledge, because the
many ',such cases that remain hid in privacy
cannot be made subservient to the noble
uses of moral teaching. GUERNSEY, it
has been justly said, "died in action." The
fact is so; and, moreover, the nature and the
insidents of lii calling are ouch as to make

analogy between it and military service, an
appropriate line of comment and illustration.
The same thing, or one closely similar, might ,
be said with respect to the contingencies of
several occupations; such as navigation,
mining, and other forms of employment in-
volving peril to life or limb. Whenever such
pursuits are beneficial to society, and in por-
portion as they are so, no opportunity ought to
be lost of doing fit honour to the men that
have the courage and devotedness to engage
in them. And, when they are overtaken by
dangers that result in death, it is impossible
to pay them, in mere honours, more than they
deserve, while a proper sense of gratitnde
dictates the obligation to adopt, as the sacred
care :of the community, the widows and
orphans of those who, thus dying, leave such
dependants behind them.
The fact that these classes of our fellow-
men who face death, and often meet with it,
in the ordinary discharge of daily duty, receive
wages, takes nothing from the amount of the ob-
ligation under which they lie who are exempt
from the danger yet enjoy the benefit. What are
those wages? Trivial indeed when weighed
in the scale against the mortal contingencies
every day in prospect. Only consider what
may at any moment happen, and, in some
labours, such as mining, what is actually and
constantly attendant ; and how can the
willingness of uncounted numbers in every
generation to take such employments, be
understood except by crediting them with a
noble contempt of danger, an exalted spirit of
self-denial, and a magnanimous devotion to
the broad interests of their fellow-men, as the
highest rule of conduct between men and
men? The truth is, that men and women
who attain to the highest point of Christian
perfection of which human nature is sus-
ceptible in this life, nearly always reach
that grand elevation without valuing
themselves at all upon it; they being
themselves, in fact, always the last
to think anything at all about it, often,
indeed, thinking of themselves as less than
the least of all who have good in them, while
other men, who have any spice of sympathy,
are lost in admiration of their shining nobility
of character. This high style of moral merit
cannot be arrogated to any class or order of
men to the exclusion of the rest. Happily
for the world bright specimens of it are to be
found in every class and order. It is to be
observed, however, that such specimens are
most numerous among those who compose the
bulk of the community, partly because they
are in millions while others are but in hun-
dreds, but, also, because it is these masses of
mankind who furnish the men that at the
lowest rate of recompense accept the heaviest
toil, and face the most imminent and most
deadly dargers.y The ought not to be ex-
pected to work too hard, and, for their hard
and dangerous work, they ought to be amply
and ungrudgingly paid. In so far, however,
as they hazard life for the common good,
they ask for nothing, and, in truth,
nothing that might be given could repay
them. Nevertheless, it cannot but for-
tify their courage and solace them under ex-
posure to see by such signs as a great public
funeral to a simple fireman perishing in the
performance of his perilous duty, that such
sacrifices are correspondingly appreciated.

articles.text:
THE RIGHT OF THE PEERS TO VOTE

AT ELECTIONS.

TIIE question raised the other day in the
Court of Queen's Bench on behalf of the Earl
of BEAUCIIIIIP and the Marquis of SIMSBURY
should not be carelessly or summarily dis-
missed from the public mind, namely, as to
the right of peers of the realm voting at Par-
liamentary elections.
There were five Judges on the bench, all
wigged and learned, and several gentlemen of
the long robe engaged on both sides, also
wigged and learned, and when these had
passed the thing through their hands in the
ordinary way, the decision was given against
the claim of both nobleman in a very clear
and decided manner. From what the LORD
CHIEF JUSTICE said in giving judgment, it is
clear "that it is a high infringement of the
privileges of Parliament for any peer to inter-

fere in the election of members of Parlia-
ment."

There can be no doubt of the law on this
point, and now that this has been made clear
to the two noble personages who raised the
question, the further consideration arises as
to whether this law should not be altered, and
precisely the same right given to peers that are
enjoyed by the ordinary voters who are simply
when taken altogether called the " Commons "
of England. What is gained by this exclu-
sion? It is true peers cannot legally vote,
but in the boroughs, cities, and counties of
England, the simple votes of the peers when
spread over the whole of the constituencies
would be neutralized by an equivalent number
of the most ragged of the unwashed.

Practically, to be deprived of the vote is not
much of a hardship to the peers of England,
and whatever it amounts to as an injustice
does not seem to have affected their 'well-
being as a class. Beyond this, is it not true
that the exclusion of the peers from inter-
fering with our Parliamentary elections is one
of the merest figments of the imagination. The
British "Constitution " very likely means
practical exclusion, but history and experience
both prove to us that they were never excluded.
From the earliest election down to the latest
this general truth holds good. Let any reader
open Dob's "Parliamentary Companion," and
he may see how the various constituencies arc
influenced, and who holds the power to secure
the return of candidates. One of our last
elections was at Richmond, in Yorkshire, and
there a candidate came forward, not to oppose
his rival on political grounds, but to vindicate
the independence of the borough from the
domination of the Earl of ZETLAND, and got
defeated as a matter of course. Richmond is
yet in the hands of the Earl of ZETLAND as
completely as if the law of exclusion did not
exist. Why should this man, therefore, make
a disturbance about not having a vote, when
he carries a seat in his pocket which he.might
bestow on his butler or groom if ho thought
fit?

It is difficult to believe that the peers, as a
body, will be grateful to the Marquis of
SALISBURY or Earl BEAUCHAMP for stirring
up this question of peers' rights. The old
adage "let well enough alone," applies very
strongly in this case. Between the peers of
England and the Commons of England there
is an old and a very long account to settle.
If the Commons of England withhold any
right front the peers it should be at once con-
ceded—the people have no desire to oppress
the peers; and as they have to submit to taxa-
tion imposed by a body in the election of which
they have no right to vote, that right should
be conferred on them without loss of time. If
thelaw as it stands withholds this, as it clearly
does, the law should be a4ered by the action
of Liberal politicians. In many matters as
well as this our concern is more with what we
have power to make the law do than with a
disputed definition of what it does. We can
alter the law so as to give the peers what in its
present state it denies thorn. If their present
exclusion is really inoperative in the largest
and most important sense, why higgle about
the fraction now in dispute? If they kayo got
the whole animal except the tail, let that be
thrown to them also, and then as British
citizens they cannot say in the Court of
Queen's Bench or elsewhere that one jot or
tittle of their rights as British citizens is with-
held from them. The people will then have
discharged their duties in full, and may
turn to the other side of the account and
examine into the item of privileges with a view
to its settlement.

In these circumstances the general question
may be put as to the value of exolusive
privileges in a State. Why should we have
such an institution as a House of Lords?
Why the privileges belonging to an aris
tocratie class ? It is not necessary to
suggest a sweeping away of our House ot
Lords, but when certain of the members of
that assembly challenge the country on a
question of right, it is practically an invitation
to open up the whole question.. Aristocracies
keep their ground now only in those States
where ancient barbarism holds most influence
by law and custom. The Ashantee noble,
bedizened in the cast-off clothes of our LOUD

MA.Yon'.B coachman or footman, is still safe in
possession of his privileges. In Europe these
come every day more and more in question.
The masses suffering from ignorance and want
are unfitted to take part in public affairs, and
need, therefore, cultivated and privileged
classes to guide and control them. The same
masses growing in education, comfort, and
independence, require no such leadership, and
are everywhere murmuring at its existence.
The growth of civilisation, and the increase
and diffusion of wealth, mean, also, the growth
and diffusion of right, of law, of liberty, of
justice, and these are not fully attainable in
the presence of a favoured caste.
Primogeniture and entail are necessary to
the existence of a feudal aristocracy, and we
should ask ourselves whether we ought to
foster such institutions for the benefit of a
class. We shall have to dig deep to find the
true causes of our dangerous social inequali-
ties, and if, when we have done so, we dis-
cover that the operation of the laws, made
in the interest of an aristocracy, encourages
these inequalities, and aggravates their worst
evils, they will be attacked and destroyed
without fear or remorse. There would be use
in an aristocracy, and a House of Lords, were
they composed of the "wisest and the best,"
and if their desire was to promote the public
welfare. When that is made clear, it will not
be difficult to fall in with the common notion.
But if they can furnish no acceptable proof
that such is the case, their existence is an
anomaly in the State without sufficient justifi-
cation. It is understood that this privileged
class may be recruited from the ablest and
best, but virtue and wisdom have not hitherto
been the tests of fitness for admission to seats
in our Upper House. Our history for the
last century has not been a blank. Ministers
of the Crown held out bribes of title to the
influential and wealthy, and secured their
support against the nation by conferring on
them the dignities and privileges of a caste,
and the expectancy of such bribes has had a
strong influence in keeping the rich at the
command of those in power.
The present movement in Prussia, unmis-
takably demonstrates the fact, that the aristo-
cracy as a privileged class is on its trial before
other tribunals than those set up by the com-
mon sense and policy of the people. The
King of PRUSSIA and Prince BISMARCK, in
striking at the power of the Prussian nobility,
it is right to believe, are actuated by con-
siderations of national requirements, more
than by blind democratic passions. People
everywhere are discovering that an "aristo-
cracy in the nineteenth century is the league,
the coalition of those who wish to consume
without producing, live without working,
occupy all public places without becoming
competent to fill them, and seize upon all
honours without meriting them." It is well
that the Marquis of SALISBURY and Earl
BEAUCHAMP have raised the question as to the
rights of our peers, and it is to be hoped that
the people will grant these, and at the same
time, in the interest of the State, take from
them those privileges which in so many ways
interfere with the prosperity and progress of
the masses of the people.

articles.title: LONDON POLICE.
articles.text:
THE LONDON POLICE.

Ounwr policemen to agitate? If so, they
may be left to the power and strategy they
possess for the assertion and maintenance of
their rights. If not, those who hold authority
over them should carefully take note of their
requirements and concede all reasonable de-
mands before dissatisfaction gives birth to in-
subordination. If it be absolutely necessary
that the police should 'always be at the com-
mand of the authorities without question of
any kind on their parts, it is just as desirable
that the men belonging to the force should not
in any way be arbitrarity or unjustly treated.

This week we have had a mutiny of the police
in a very mild way. The men at Kensington
station when mustered, refused in a body to
go on duty on the ground that a brother police.
man bad been drafted into another, and pre-
sumably inferior position, because he had
acted as their secretary in the combined
action they had taken for the purpose
of securing an advance of pay. The
newspapers have made mom than the era-

nary amount of fuss about this, and much
blame has been cast upon the men; but we
have no hesitation in saying that the fault is
altogether on the other side. The dis-
missal of GOODCIIILD, the secretary,
may be taken as the real cause of
the disturbance, and it may be remarked that
such dismissals are the cause of a considerable
number of disputes between employers and
employed. It is a mean and dastardly act to
take advantage of men who act thus in the
interest of their fellows. It is simply a childish
revenge, and the man who commits such
an act, be he employer of labourer or com-
missioner of police, is a contemptible tyrant,
to whom. the management of men ought not
to be entrusted.

In regularly- organized bodies of workmen
the secretary is a person with whom em-
ployers have no power to deal; they do not
engage him, and they have no right therefore
to discharge him. But where a union is im-
provised, as amongst post-office servants,
railway employes, persons in the employment
of the Government, or "policemen, ho who
acts as secretary, or in any way takes a
prominent part in their proceedings, however
reasonable their demands, is sure to be pounced
on by those in authority and sacrificed as an
example and a warning.

Whatever Sub-Commissioner Colonel LABLL-
IIONDIERE may say to the contrary, we shall
believe that the conduct of the authorities to-
wards 000DCI1TLD was a consequence of the
action he had taken on behalf of the men, and
that it was meant as a persecution to worry
him out of the force. The ease is a very com-
mon case; it has occurred hundreds of times
amongst our working men, and whatever the
consequence to the public, it is the duty of
the men in the force to protect each other, or
they never can possibly by joint action remedy
any wrong they may labour under. Instead
of persecuting and ruining those who act for
the men, the authorities ought to recognise
them and discuss with them anything they
may have to complain of. In this way a
friendly intercourse between them and those
above them might be kept up, and by a kind
of constant arbitration harmony might be pre-
served throughout the force, and strikes, as
expressions of difference, rendered difficult, if
not impossible.
Instead of reasonable action of this kind,
any man who moves as a leader amongst his
fellow is picked out with a view to his destruc-
tion; and resistance, therefore, becomes a
matter of duty on the part of those for whom
he acts, which it would_bo an utter meanness
not to enter on.

There is now a contagion of resistance to op-
pres-sion amongst working men. The fig ht has
been fought out in every branch of industry,
and won by the workers. Policemen are the
instruments of power, the extinguishers by
which resistance is smothered; now the ex-
tinguishers themselves have taken fire, and
will require more skill to put out than com-
missioners and sub-commissioners seem to
possess.

articles.title: REV. J. J. MANLEY AND DISESTA-
articles.text:
REV. J. J. MANLEY AND DISESTA-

BLISIIMENT.

WE published last week in the BEE -Hivr,
an account of an attack made by the Rev. J.
J. MANLEY at a meeting of the Church Defence
Association at Birmingham on Mr. G. POTTER,
which, from beginning to end, had not in it one
word of truth. It was delivered before a crowded
meeting, was applauded to the echo, and was,
taken altogether, as good a specimen as need
be of those triumphant victories gained by
such abusive champions as take a pleasure in
triumphing over monsters of their own crea-
tion.

There can be no objection that friends of the
Church should defend it. Indeed, it is right
that men like the Rev. J. 3. JSlss-LEY, who live
by it, should do battlo for it when it is at-
tacked. Whatever it may be to others, it is a
blessing to them. It finds them in bread and
butter, and beef and mutton—it puts clothes
en their backs, and, keeps a roof over their
heads—and, provides them with comfortable
bed and blankets. They may believe in the
Established Church as an exponent of the
highest truth, but they must believe in it as
the bountif4 giver of loaves and fisheg.

But if others refrain from attributing selfish
motives to them, they certainly ought not to be
forward in impugning the motives of their an-
tagonists. There are no men more open to
charges of selfishness and hypocrisy than
clergymen, and none would be so subject to
them if others were as uncharitable and reck-
less in statement as they usually are. It is
too frequently the case that persons who are
not subject to contradiction are waspish and
ill-natured when they meet with those not
willing to take their statements for granted.
The Rev. J. J. MANLEY is clearly one of these.
Ile does not feel under any necessity to ob-
serve the ordinary rules of good manners. He
makes his charges without enqu;ring, or, per-
haps, oaring, whether they are true or not.
He calumniates in quite an off-hand cheerful
way, and goes through a string of untruths
with the effrontery of a quack at a fair puffing
his unwholesome wares.

The friends of the Church, lay and clerical,
should avoid such disreputable practices.
They only take effect for a time. The Rev.
J. J. ItA.NLEY was possibly pleased with the
applause at the moment, and might have re-
tired from the meeting of his Church friends
under the impression that he had done the in-
stitution by which he is fed a service. We
are curious to find out how he will attempt to
justify himself, now that the public have dis-
covered by means of the Birmingham papers
how untrue every separate point of his
charge is.
This, however, is his business; but as it
may not be his first offence, and as custom
may have made slander in him a "property of
easiness," he may go on defending his Church
by bearing false witness against his neigh-
bours. If so, something more than simple
contradiction may be necessary to stop the
wagging of his mendacious tongue. It would
be dangerous to allow such a person to go
about without giving him some kind of warn-
ing as to the obligations he is under to truth.

We are anxious that the discussion on the
disendowment and the disestablishment of the
Church should be carried on in a spirit of
courtesy and fairness. If all who engage in
it, however, should follow the Rev. J. J.
MANLEY'S example, and make it a noisy hub-
bub of falsehood and misrepresentation, the
public may have to extinguish it, were it only
to get rid of such a nuisance.

articles.title: AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.
articles.text:
THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.

A CONFERENCE of the London Consultative
Committee of the National Agricultural La-
bourers' Union was held on Friday, at Bolt-
court, Fleet•street, Mr. GEORGE POTTER in
the chair, to make arrangements for holding a
mass meeting at Exeter Hall, the special object
of which is to enlist the sympathy of the work-
ing classes of London on behalf of the Agri-
cultural Labourers. It is proposed that the
meeting shall ,be held on Tuesday, 10th of
December. As hitherto there has been no im-
portant meeting in the metropolis connected
with the movement of the peasants for an
amelioration of their social condition, it is be-
lieved that the great question, which is so
strongly moving in the provinces, cannot be
indifferent to the great mass of Londoners.
London, in fact, reflects the opinion of the
whole country, and the London Press is the
chief medium for the expression of public
opinion.
The CIIA.IRMAN informed the meeting that
a deputation had waited upon the LORD
MAYOR to ask his Lordship to preside at the
proposed meeting at Exeter Hall; and
ho had consented to take the chair.
Deputations had also waited upon Mr.
SAMUEL MORLEY, M.P., Dr. MANNING, and
Rev. Canon GIRDLESTONE, all of whom have
promised to take part in the meeting.
Mr. Ana, President of the National Agri-
cultural Labourers' Union, Was present at the
meeting, and stated that himself and other
farm labourers would attend the Exeter Hall
demonstration, and represent the Labourers'
Union.

The Daily Telegraph of Thuradav, in an
article on the proposed meeting, says

"On the second Tuesday of next month ono
most important step is to be taken in narrowing a
hitherto vague and diffusive argument to tangible
proportions. On that evening AU aggrepto meet.;

ing of the working men of London will be held
at Exeter Hall, with the Lord Mayor in the chair,
and the assemblage will be addressed by a num-
ber of gentlemen:peculiarly qualified to speak with
authority on the matter in hand. Who, for
example, will question the claims of Sir Sydney
Waterlow to be heard with the deepest attention
in any discussion concerning the well-being of the
poor I' And equally valuable will be the testimony
of Archbishop Manning, whose pastoral duties
bring him in constant contact with those whose
lot it is to labour and to suffer. The names of Mr.
Samuel Morley, M.P., of Mr. Arundella, 31. P., and
of the Rev. Canon Girdlestone, speak for them-
selves. Sir John Bennett, again, should be
able to render very efficient service to the cause.
He is not only a large employer of the mechanical
labour needed in his London business, but a prac-
tical agriculturist—a gentleman farmer, sowing
and reaping on his own account in Sussex, and
thus necessarily acquainted with the capacity and
the wants of the rural workman. There are few
persons who know more about work and working
men in London than Mr. George Potter, and the
opposite polo of that labour will be aptly repre-
sented by Mr. Guile, Mr. Mitchell, and especially
by Mr. Arch, the President of the Agricultural
Labourers' Union. We hold the proposed meet-
ing to be one of which the result should be
thoroughly practical—first, as laying the bases for
some definite scheme of action by which the con-
dition of the rustic labourer maybe at once
ameliorated; and next, as calculated to extract
from the working men .of London a genuine
expression of opinion and of sympathy with
their brethren in the country. The time has
gone by to prate about the innocence of
rural life, and the unsophisticated nature of the
countryman, about property having its duties as
well as its rights,' about the kind pressure of
the social chain,' and platitudes of that kind.
They may be very good adjuncts to after-dinner
oratory, and may sweeten the doses of advice
offered at Ritualistic harvest homes; but the
question which will be brought before a hard-
headed audience on the 10th of next month is
essentially one pertaining to political economy ; it
is a question of work and wages. The worth of
anything,' we are told by the great master of
rhymed wisdom, is just as much as it will bring.'
To that postulate we must needs adhere; yet the
time has arrived for the country seriously and
sternly to ask whether the labour of the peasant
is not a great deal more valuable than it has been
assumed to be; whether it would not be worth a
good deal more if exported by wholesale to another
market; and whether it would not bring much
more even at home were not the wages of
labourers kept down by something like systematic
combination between the landlords and farmers."

" FAGGING " AND " TUNDING."

Tug oorrespondence ,in the press, relative
to " fagging " and. " tunding " at our great
publio schools, possesses an interest for others
besides those who send their children to such
establishments. The description given by
persons who have written to the papers, and
who, as a rule, speak from personal experience
of the punishments inflicted, the kind of per-
sons who administer them, the instruments
used, and the causes which lead to them, are
a curious mixture of the cruel and grotesque.
We have nothing to say against the general
efficiency of the system pursued at the Win-
chester School. The masters;may be gentle-
men of great learning, deep piety, and un-
questionable humanity. They may desire to
perform the difficult duties of their positions
with as much benefit as possible to those
placed under their charge. Still there should
be no hesitation in declaring that under what-
ever sense of duty they may act, the tyranny
practiced in the establishment to which they
belong is utterly abominable in its character,
and the punishments inflicted on boys under
such a system cannot but degrade and brutify
their characters. Let any person of decent
habits think for a moment of punishing a boy
by blows of an ash sapling because he does
not know the slang names used in the schoo
for things and places. Just imagine a pool
boy being compelled to stoop and hold his toes
whilst a young ruffian callea a " prefect "
beats him with a stick on the lower part of his
back—a punishment called "Wading." A
correspondent in the Telegraph, under the
signature of "FRANK," declares that two
college prefects, a short time ago, so thrashed
and bullied a wretched inferior that he abso-
lutely went out of his mind for some days;
that On one occasion forty jgniors were Dente u

Nov. 23, 187

with a ground-ash stick by one prefect; and
that to sixty boys during this autumn alone
over one hundred lickings were administered.

Let us not forget that these are not persons
of low birth or degraded calling—they are the
sons ofgentlemen; and those in authority who
allow these brutalities to be practiced are gen-
tlemen and scholars, and ought, in what they
do and in what they allow to be done, to be
influenced by a sense of humanity and man-
liness such as is presumed to prevail in
society at the present day.
We do not desire to limit our public
teachers in such power as may be necessary to
enforce discipline, but the brutal beating of
one boy by another is not necessary for this,
and every father of a family, in fact every
man and woman of ordinary humanity, must
be convinced that such is the case. What
would be said, we may ask, if such things
were practiced in the workshops of the country
on the part of men towards the apprentices
they have to teach, and with whom they have
occasionally much trouble? A few such eases
would, if exposed, at once excite the horror
and indignation of all right-thinking per-
sons," and spread the conviction that the
working men of the country were so barbarous
and brutal in their manners as to need the
restraints of law. If a boy in any workshop
in England was ordered to hold his toes after
the fashion of the poor wretches at Win-
chester, that he might have a stick applied to
his bent body, the fellow who struck him
would be kicked from the workshop by his
brother workers without hesitation or pity.
In truth such a practice could not bear the
light of day for an hour amongst our working
people. Old and venerable as it may be, even our
operative Conservatives would rise up against
it, for though their political insight is not to
be relied on or admired, there is no reason to
suspect in them a want of the ordinary man-
liness and humanity of their class.

It is really not worth while to mention the
name of the head-master at Winchester. The
practices that prevail there exist elsewhere in
our public schools, and just as it was right to
legislate against the brutal practices of cock-
fighting, bull-baiting, and overwork of chil-
dren in factories, it is necessary to at once
put down by law these cruel practices, which
are disgraceful in themselves, and in many
ways injurious to the country, as we can
neither neglect the children of the poor, nor
brutalize the children of the rich, without
paying heavily for such sins of omission and
commission.

articles.title: WIND FALLS.
articles.text:
WIND FALLS.

AN old woman named linowN died the other
day at the West-end of London, leaving be-
hind her, without will or any intimation ef
any kind as to its application and use,
£250,000. This sum has fallen to the
CHANCELLOR of the ExcraquEn, and will go
to defray the ordinary expenses of Govern-
ment. Mr. LOWE, no doubt, will be very
much pleased to receive it, and so far as it
goes, it will, as a drop in the bucket, do
something in adding to the resources of the
State.

We do not know how Mrs. Bnowsr got her
money, but we do know that a multitude Of
BROWNS, 83LETIL9, and others, whom) ziarel

are not worth remembering, have, within the
last century, got hundreds of millions of
pounds sterling as profit from the work of
poor wretches who for the most part have died
in our workhouses and have been buried in
parish shells. Mrs. BROWN had not, it would
appear, any disposition to make a will.
Thousands upon thousands of poor wretches
were hungering around her, but Mrs. Bnowx,
with her quarter of a million, allowed them to
hunger; she had more money than she knew
what to do with, but she had. "no "to
clothe the naked, to educate tho ignorant,
to help the struggling, or to lift up the
fallen. She was simply a wretched old
creature called Mrs. BROWN, who could have
done many good things, but preferred not doing
them, and whose wealth in consequence has
gone, without diminution, into the ever-open
hands of the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER;
or perhaps she did sympathise kindly, and
helped liberally, but died, nevertheless, with
this huge surplus.
Still, a very proper question, we think, might
bo raised here, as to whether some different
use should not be found for money falling thus
into the coffers of the State. Few people owe
much to the Exchequer. The tax gatherer is
not in the habit of allowing miserly people to
make default if he can prevent it, and though,
no doubt, false returns are sometimes made to
the hurt of the revenue, it is a matter between
those who pay and receive which has to be
corrected or prevented by the best practicable
means the authorities can set in motion. For
one offender of this kind, however, there are
thousands who offend against the charitable
duties of life; who, having a superabundance
of wealth, walk daily amongst their poor
suffering brethren without any feeling of pity,
or any kindly generous impulse to suggest
their relief.
Unfeeling parsimoniousness of this kind
cannot be corrected by law; society gives to
individuals the means to enormously accumu-
late, but it cannot give to certain of these the
disposition to distribute liberally for the relief
of the poor. This being the case, should not
the vast sums hoarded by the sordid, and
left without appropriation by will, be devoted
after: their death to purposes of benevolence?
The money left behind them by such intestates
would make a grand fund which might be
used in many ways to succour tho distressed
and aid the struggling. The duties such
persons neglected. to do whilst living might
be performed. by means of their money after
death, and might, if turned to such use, not
only do a vast amount of good to poor persons,
but might oven ho as useful to themselves as
the sums which in the olden times were
devoted to religious purposes on behalf of the
souls of those who left them with a view to
their eternal welfare. We throw this out as
a hint to our law-makers, but without the
least hope that they will notice it. To labour
for the welfare of the poor is no special mission
of theirs, except when by so doing they in-
crease their power in Parliament.

articles.title: CRISIS IN FRANCE.
articles.text:
THE CRISIS IN FRANCE.

_
GAIDErrA. seems to be the only conspicuous
man in Franco who is at the same time high-
principled and discreet. Without doubt, he
shines by comparison with the subtle, yet
bewildered old gentleman whose great rival he
is supposed to be. M. DREES, however, has
the advantage, on his side, of comparison, or
contrast rather, with both the men who try to
prostrate him and the other men who, in
certain drawing-rooms at Paris, are freely
spoken of as his fractional successors. It will
not be known, we gather, before Monday bow
the present uncertainty is to eventuate; but
among those whom self-interest is regarded as
gifting with the keenest foresight, it is calcu-
lated that the threatening storm will blew
over. It is never safe, however, to rely upon
attempts to anticipate issues, which attempts
have no surer guide than the sordid instincts
of the Paris Bourse.
Everyone can easily believe that a man of
M. advanced age becomes tired of
work, when, instead of being steady and un-
hindered effort towards a fixed and useful end,
the workman is harassed and embarassed at
every step, and that on both sides at once.
When, however, ho meets euch obstacles by

endeavouring to steer a sinuous way between
the opposite parties from which they come,
the attendant consequences are sure to be
little satisfactory to his peace and progress.
In fact, the further he goes in a tedious and
merely expediential course, the tunes of his
temper are pretty sure to become only more
and severer.

Let the PRESIDENT of the REPUBLIC settle
it in his own mind on what terms, and with
what views he will carry on the Government;
and the right party, strong as it is in num-
bers and hot in temper, will crumble into
the heterogeneous atoms of which it is really
composed. If he could persuade politicians
to limit themselves in paying the war indem-
nity, and freeing the soil of France from the
foot of the conqueror, his sincere, earnest,
constant, and. able efforts in that direction are
enough to keep him in his seat so long as
health and strength might hold him upright
in it. But, with apparently the single ex-
ception of GIIEBETTA, party DIEM of all shades
and both sides are far too eager and impatient
to wait till that work, absolutely necessary
and urgently pressing as it is, has been accom-
plished. As for M. TIIIEDS calling, as he
does, for a vote of confidence, he must decide
for himself, and openly avow both what will
satisfy him, and to what he will bind himself in
order to insure it. What lease of power would he
have? What would he do with the existing
Assembly? To what form of settled Govern-
ment does he look? To talk about President-
ship for life when so old a man is in question
is scarcely more than a prolongation of power
from one birth-day to another. If he is not
prepared for a total Dissolution, why not
a renewal of the Assembly by degrees?
This would be not simply a compro-
mise between the tenacity of the Rurals
and the clean sweep ardently desired
by the Radicals, but it would afford an
opportunity for public opinion to express it-
self, from time to time, in the elections ;
which, whatever violent prrtisans might say,
would be a valuable guide to statesmen
honestly desirous of the public good. At
present, as the Into returns from several
departments indisputably showed, the learn-
ing of the national mind is towards the Re-
publican form of Government; a periodical
series of elections spread early on the country
would either confirm, or modify, perhaps even
contradict, this manifestation of sentiment.
Upon the whole, it would be one way of avoid-
ing those convulsions which attend sudden
and complete changes. Observers may well
admire the masterly silence af GAMBETTI. It
shows confidence in his principles, and a wise
willingness to be carried forward over rough
places without needless efforts of his own.

GONE HOME.
He stands in the door of his cottage—
He with the silver hair—
Thinking of youth's lost summer,
When life seemed bright and fair.
The trees are folding their branches
Around that gray old roof,'
And the sunbeam merrily mingles
Its gold with their sombre woof.
He thinks, as be stands in the doorway,
Of a sweet and pure young life
That ho had fondly cherished—
His darling, trusting wife;
How he won her in her girlhood,
And praised her beauty rare.
And her silvery laughter cheered him
When his soul was racked with care.
He thinks of the angel at midnight,
Stealing o'er the threshold stone,
Taking his treasure from him,
And leaving him all alone;
He thinks of the graceful willow
That waves above her form;
And wonders why he lingers,
Since the loved one is now gone.
• 6 • • • *

Twilight is fast approaching,
And closed is the cottage door;
Ho with the locks of silver
Will stand in its shade no more.
Like golden drops of music,
Like the echo of silver bells,
Through the trees the winds' low mu' Emu:
A tale of sadness tells.

Again in watches of midnight,
Over that threshold stone,
Has the angel been with a message
To bear the old man home—
Home, where his bride is waiting;
Home, to that beautiful clime,
Where sorrow for ever ceases,
Where love shall outlive e'en time.
L. H.

COMMON SENSE.
She came among the gathering crowd,
A maiden fair, without pretense;
And when they asked her humble name,
She whispered, mildly, "Common Sense."
Her modest garb drew every eye,
Her ample cloak, her shoes of leather;
And, when they sneered, she simply said,
"I dress according to the weather."
They argued long and reasoned loud
In dubious Hindoo phrase mysterious;
While she, poor child could not divine
Why girls so young should be so serious.
They knew the length of Plato's beard,
And bow the scholars wrote in Saturn;
She studied authors not so deep,
And took the Bible for her pattern.
And so she said, "Excuse me, friends,
I find all, have their proper places,
And Common Sense should stay at home
With cheerful hearts and smiling faces."
C. B.

articles.title: lINFORGOT TEN WORDS.
articles.text:
lINFORGOT TEN WORDS.

"Have you examined that bill, James P"
"Yea, Sir."
"Anything wrong ?"
"I find two errors."

" Ah ! let me see."
The lad handed his employer a long bill that
had been placed on his desk for examination.
"Here is an error in the calculation of two
sovereigns, which they have made against them-
selves; and another error of two sovereigns in the
adding up."
"Also arinst themselves r'
"Yes, Sir."
The merchant smiled in a way that struck the
lad as peculiar.
":Four pounds against themselves !" he re-
marked, in a kind of pleasant surprise. "Trusty
clerks they must have ! "
"Shall I correct the figures ? " asked the lad.
"No; let them correct their own mistakes. We
don't examine bills fur other people's benefit," re-
plied the merchant. "It will be time enough for
us to rectify these errors when they find them out.
All so much gain, as it now stands.
The boy's delicate moral sense was shocked at
so unexpected a remark. He was the son of a
poor widow' who had given him good instruction
and taught him that to be just was the duty of all
men. Mr. Carman, the merchant in whose em-
ployment be had been only a few months, WM an
old friend of his father's, and a person in whom
his mother reposed the highest confidence. In fact,
James had always looked upon him as a kind of
model man and when Mr. Carman agreed to take
him into his warehouse, he felt that great good
fortune was in his way.
"Let them correct their own mistakes." The
words made a strong impression on the mind of
James Lewis. When first spoken by Mr. Carman,
and with the meaning then involved, he felt, as
we have said, shocked; but as he turned them over
and over again in his thoughts, and connected
their utterance with a person who stood so high in
lib mother's estimation, ho began to think that

perhaps the thing was fair enough in business.
Mr. Carman was hardly the man to do wrong.'
In a few days after James examined the bill, a
clerk from the house by which it had been ren-
dered called for a settlement. The lad, who was
present, waited with considerable interest to see
whether Mr. Carman would speak of the error.
But he made no remark on the subject. A cheque
for the amount of the bill as rendered was filled
up, and a receipt taken.
"Is that right ?" James asked himself this
question. His moral sense said No • but the fact
that Mr. Carman had so acted bewildered his
mind.
"It may be the way in business " sole thought
with himself—" but it -don't look honest. I
wouldn't have believed it of him 1"
Mr. Carman had a kind way with him that won
upon the boy's heart, and naturally tended to
make him judge whatever he might do in the most
favourable manner. _ _

"I wish he had corrected that error," he said to
himself a great many times when thinking, in a
pleased way, of Mr. Carman and his own good
fortune in having been received into his employ-
ment. "It don't look right; but may be it's the
way in business."
One day he went to the bank and drew the money
for a cheque. In counting it over he found that
the clerk had paid him ten pounds too much. So
he went back to the counter and told him of the
mistake. The clerk thanked him, and he returned
to the warehouse with the pleasant consciousness
in his mind of having done right.
"The clerk overpaid me by ten pounds," ho
said to Mr. Carman, as ho handed him the money.
"Indeed !" replied the latter, a light breaking
over his countenance. And he hastily counted
the bank-notes.

The light faded as the last note left his fingers.
"There's no mistake, James." A tone of dis-
appointment was in his voice.
"Oh ! I gave back the ten pounds. Wasn't
that right?"
"You simpleton !" exclaimed Mr. Carman.
"Don't you know that bank mistakes are never
corrected? If the clerk had paid you ten
sovereigns short he would not have made it
right."
The warm blood, stained the cheeks of James
under this reproof. It is often the ease that more
shame is felt for a blunder than a crime. In this
instance the lad felt a sense of mortification at
having done what Mr. Carman was pleased to call
a silly thing; and he made up his mind that if
they should overpay him a hundred pounds at the
bank he Would bring the amount to his employer,
and lot him do as he pleased with the money.
"Let people look after their own mistakes,"
said Mr. Carman.

James Lewis pondered these things in his
heart. The impression they made was too strong
ever to be forgotten. "It may be right," he said
to himself, but he did not feel altogether satisfied.
A. month or two after the occurrence of that
bank mistake, as James counted over his weekly
wages, just received from Mr. Carman, he dis-
covered that he had paid half-a-crown too much.
The first impulse of his mind was to return the
amount to his employer, and it was on his lip to
say, "You have given me too much, sir," when
the unforgotten words, "Let people look after
their own mistakes," flashed upon his thoughts,
and made him hesitate. To hold a parley with
evil is, in most cases, to be overcome.

"I must think about this," said James, as he
put the money into his pocket. "If it is true in
one ease, it is true in another. Mr. Carman don't
correct mistakes that people make in his favour;
and he can't complain when the rule works
against himself."
But the boy was very far from being in a corn-
fortable state. Ho felt that to keep that half-
crown would be a dishonest act. Still he could
not make up his mind to return it; at least not
then. He would retain it for the present, and
think the matter over more carefully. He could,
if the case did not prove clear on further reflection,
make all right with himself and Mr. Carman.

To hold—a
parley with evil is, as we have just
said, in Most oases to be overcome; and it was un-
happily so in the present case. James did not re-
turn the half-crown, but spent it for his own grati-
fication. After he had done this it came suddenly
into his thought that Mr. Carman might only be
trying him and he was filled with anxiety and
alarm, liow bitterly did he regret having spent
the money. For two or three days it was as much
as he could do to keep from starting when Mr.
Carman spoke to him; or to look steadily into his
face when receiving from hire any direction. It
was his first sad experience in wrong-doing. But
as no lack of confidence was exhibited James felt
re-assured in a few days.
Not long afterwards Mr. Carman repeated the
same mistake. This time James kept the half-
crown with less hesitation.
"Let him correct his own mistakes," said he,
resolutely; "that's the doctrine he acts on with
other people, and he can't complain if he gets paid
in the coin he puts in circulation. I just wanted
half-a-crown.

From this time the fine moral sense of James
Lewis was blunted. He had taken an evil coun-
sellor into his heart, who not only darkened his
clear perceptions of right but stimulated a spirit
of oovetousness—latent in almost every mind—
and caused him to desire the possession of things
beyond his ability to obtain.
James had good business qualities, and so pleased
Mr. Carman by his intelligence, industry, and tact
with customers, that he advanced him rapidly, and
gave him, before he was eipteen years of age, the
most responsible position in his warehouse. But
James had learned something more from his em-
ployer than how to do business well. He had
learned to be dishonest—that is the word. He had
never forgotten the first lesson he received in this
bad science; and he had acted upon it not only in
two instances, but in a hundred, and almost
always to the injury of Mr. Carman. He had
long since given up waiting for mistakes to be
ade ji his favour, but originated them in the
,R

varied and complicated transactions of a large
business in which he was trusted implicitly; for,
strangely enough, it had never for an instant
occurred to Mr. Carman that his failure to be just
to the letter in dealing might prove a snare to this
young man.
James grew sharp, cunning, and skilful; always
on the alert; always bright; always prompt to
meet any approaches to a discovery of his wrong.
dealing towards his employer, who held him in the
highest regard.
Thus it went on until James Lewis was in his
twentieth year, when the merchant had his suspi-
cions aroused by a letter that spoke of the young
man as not keeping the most respectable company,
and as spending money too freely for a clerk on a
moderate salary. Before this time James had re-
moved his mother into a pleasant house, for which
he paid a rent of sixty poun is. His salary was
one hundred and fifty; buthe deceived his mother
by telling her that ho received three hundred.
Every comfort that she needed was fulls supplied,
and she *as beginning to feel that after a long
and often painful struggle with the world her hap-
pier days had come.
James was at his desk when the letter just re-
ferred to was received by Mr. Carman. Guilt is
always on the alert, and suspicion of every move-
ment that may involve betrayal or exposure. He
looked stealthily at his employer as he opened the
letter, and observed him change countenance sud-
denly. He read it over twice, and James saw that
the contents, whatever they were, produced dis-
turbance. While he was,yet observing him, Mr.
Carman glanced toward his desk, and their eyes
met; it was only for a moment, but the look James
received made his heart atop beating.
There was something about the movements of
Mr. Carman for the rest of this day that troubled
the young man. It was plain to him that suspi•
don had been aroused by that letter. Oh, how
bitterly now did he repent, in dread of discovery
and punishment, the evil of which he had been
guilty! Exposure would disgrace and ruin him,
and bow the head of his mother, it might be, oven
to the grave.
"You are not well this evening," said Mrs.
Lewis, as she looked at her eon's changed face
across the tea-table, and noticed that he did not
eat.
"My head aches," he replied, as he turned partly
away from his mother's direct gaze.
"Perhaps the tea will make you feel better."
".I'll lie down on the sofa in the parlour for a
short time," said the young man, rising from the
table. "A little quiet may give relief." And he
went from the dining-room.
Mrs. Lewis followed him into the parlour in a
little while, and sitting down by the sofa on which
he was lying placed her hand upon his head. Ah,
it would take more than the loving pressure of a
mother's hand to ease the pain from which he was
suffering. The touch of that pure hand increased
the pain to agony.
"Do you feel better ?" asked Mrs. Lewis, after
she had remained for some time with her hand on
his forehead.

"Not much," he replied; and rising as he
spoke he added, "I think a walk in the open air
will do me good."
"Don't go out, James," said Mrs. Lewis, a
troubled feeling coming into her heart.
"I'll only walk a short distance." And James
went from the parlour, and, taking up his hat,
passed into the street without another word.
"There's something more than headache the
matter with him," was the thought of Mrs. Lewis,
and the slight feeling of trouble she had ex-
perienced began deepening into a strange concern
that involved a dread of coming evil.
For half an hour James walked without any
purpose in his mind beyond escape from the
presence of his mother. Every phase of Mr.
Carman's manner towards him after the receipt of
that letter was reviewed and dealt on, in order if
possible to determine whether suspicion of wrong-
dealing was entertained. At last his aimless walk
brought him into the neighbourhood of Mr. Car-
man's warehouse, and in passing he was surprised
at seeing a light within.
"What can this mean ?" he asked himself, a
now fear creeping, with its shuddering impulses,
into his heart. _ _ _ .

....... ..... _______
Ile went near and listened by the door and win-
dows, but could hear no sound within.
"There's something wrong," he said. "What
can it be? If this thing is discovered, what will
be the end of it? Ruin! ruin! My poor
mother!"

The wretched young man passed on, and walked
the streets for two hours, when he returned home.
His mother met him as he entered, and inquired,
with unconcealed anxiety, if he were better. He
said yes, but with a manner that only increased
the trouble she felt, and passed up hastily to his
own room.

In the morning the strangely-altered face of
James' as he met his mother at the breakfast table,
struck alarm into her heart. He was silent, and
evaded all her questions. While they still-sat at
the table the door-bell rung loudly. The sound
startled James, and he turned his ear to listen in a
nervous way, which did not escape the observation
of his mother.
"Who is it P'' asked Mrs. Lewis, as
the servant
came back from the door.
"A gentleman wishes to see Mr. James, re-
plied the girl.
James rose instantly, and went into the hall,
shutting the dining-room door as he did so. Mrs.
Lewis sat, in almost breathless expectation, await-
ing her son's return. She beard him coming back
in a few moments; but he did not enter the dining-
room. Then he returned to the street door, and
she hears it shut. All was now silent. Staiting
up, she ran out into the passage, but James was
not there. He had gone away with the person who
bad called, and witthiut a word!
Ah, that was a sad going away! Mr. Carman
had spent half the night in examining the accounts
of James, and discovered frauds to the amount of
over one thousand pounds. Blindly indignant, he
had seat an officer to arrest him early in the morn-

Xov. 28, 1872.

ing ; and it was with this officer that the unhappY
boy went away from the home of his mother never,
again to return.
"The young villain shall lie in the bed he has
made for himself!" exclaimed Mr. Carman, in his
bitter indignation. And he did not hold back in
anything, but made the exposure of the young
man's crime complete. On the trial he showed an
eager desire to have him convicted, and presented
such an array of evidence that the jury could not
give any other verdict than "Guilty."
The poor mother was in court, and audible, in
the silence that followed, came her convulsed sobs
upon the air. The presiding judge then addressed
the culprit, and asked if he had anything to say
why sentence of the law should not be pronounced
against him. All eyes were turned upon the pale/
agitated young man, who arose with an effort, and
leaned against the railing by which he stood, as if
needing the support.
" Will it please your honours," he said, "to
direct Mr. Carman, my prosecutor, to come a little
nearer, so that r can look at him and your honouts
at the same time ?"
Mr. Carman was directed to come forward to
where the boy stood. There was a breAthless
silence in the court as the prosecutor obeyed the
order, and came forward so us to be in the eyes of
all. James looked at him steadily for a few
moments, and then turned to the judges.
"What I have to say, your honours, is this
spoke calmly and distinctly—‘, and it may, in
a degree, extenuate, though it cannot excuse, my
crime. I went into that man's house an innocent
boy; and if he had been an honest man I should
not have stood before you to-day as a criminal."
Mr. Carman interrupted the young man, and
appealed to the court for protection against allege-,
tions of such an outrageous character; but he was
peremptorily ordered to be silent. James wont 011
in a firm voice.

"Only a few weeks after I went into his employ-
ment I examined a bill by his direction, and dis-
covered an error of four sovereigns.
The face of Mr. Carman crimsoned instantly.
"You remember it, I see," remarked James;
"and I shall have cause to remember it while I
live. The error was in favour of Mr. Carman, and
I asked if I should correct the figures and he
answered, 'No; let them correct their own mistakes.
We don't examine bills for other people's benefit.'
It was my first lesson in dishonesty, and I never
forgot the words. I saw the bill settled, and Mr.
Carman take four pounds that were not his own.
I felt shocked at first; it seemed such a wrong
thing. But, soon after, he called me a simpleton.
for handing back to the bank clerk ten pounds
overpaid on a cheque; and ten—"
"May I ask the protection of the Court?" said
Mr. Carman, appealing to the judges.
"Is it true what_the lad says ?" asked the pre-
siding judge.
Mr. Carman hesitated, and look confused, All
eyes were on his face; and judges, jury, lawyers,
and spectators felt certain that he was guilty of
leading the unhappy young man astray.
"Not long afterwards,' resumed young Lewis,
"in receiving my wages, I found that Mr. Carmau
had paid me a half-crown too much. I was about
giving it back to him when I remembered his re-
mark about letting people correct their own
takes, and said to myself, Let him correct his
own errors,' and dishonestly kept the money.
Again the same thing happened, and again I kept
the money that did not, of right, belong Ito me.
This was the beginning of evil, and here I sin!
Mr. Carman has shown an eagerness to convict
and have me punished, as the court has seen. If
he had shown me any mercy I might have kept
silent. But now I interpose the truth, and may
It incline you to show some consideration for Ulu
unhappiest being that is alive to-day."
The young man covered his face with his hands,
and sat down overpowered by his feelings. His
mother, who *as near him, sobbed out aloud, and
bending over, laid her hands on his head, saying,
"My poor boy! My peer boy !"
There were few eyes in the court undimmed.
In the silence that followed Mr. Carman spoke
out:

"Is my character to be thus blasted on the word
of a criminal, your honours? Is this right? Is
this just? Is this the protection a citizen finds in
this court?"

" Your solemn oath that this charge is untrue,"
said the judge, "will place you all right. It was
the unhappy boy's only opportunity, and the Court
felt bound, in humanity, to hear what he wished
to say."
James Lewis stood up again instantly, and
turned his white face and dark piercing eyes upon
Mr. Carman :
"Let him take that oath if he dare!" he ex-
claimed.
The counsel for the prosecution now interfered,
and called the proceeding an outrage on all
justice, and unheard of before in any court. But the
judge commanded order, and then said to Mr.
Carman :

" The Court offers you the only way of repara-
tion in its power. Your oath will scatter the
allegation of a criminal to the winds. Will you
swear?
Mr. Carman turned with a distressed look to-
wards his .counsel, while James kept his eye fixed
upon him. There was a brief conference, and the
lawyer said—
" The proceeding is irregular, and I have advised
my client to make no response. At the same time
he pretests against all this as an outrage upon the
rights of a citizen."
The judges bowed, and Mr. Carman withdrew.
After u brief conference with his associates, the
presiding judge said, addressing the criminal—
"In consideration of your youth, and the temp.
tation to which, in tender years, you were unhap-
pily subjected, the Court gives you its lightest
sentence, one year's imprisonment. At the sato
time, in pronouncing this sentence, let me solemnly'
warn you against any further steps in the way you
have tAken. Crime can have no valid excuse. It
is evil in the tight of God ard man, and leads only'
suff-fng. When you come forth again, after

your brief incarceration, may it be with the re-
solution to die rather than commit a crime !"
And the curtain fell on that sad scene in the
boy's life. When it lifted again, and he came
forth from prison a year afterwards, his mother
was dead. From the day her pale face faded from
his vision as he passed from the court he never
looked upon her again.
Ten years afterwards a man sat reading a news.
paper in a Far Western town. He had a calm,
serious face, and looked like one who had known
suffering and trial.
"Brought to justice at last !" ho said to himself,
as the blood came into his face. "Convicted on
tho charge of fraudulent 'insolvency, and sent to
the State's Prison! So much for the man who
gave me in tender years the first lesson in wrong.
doing! Too well, alas! did I remember his words.
But, thank God, other words have been since re-
membered. 'When you come forth again,' said
the judge, 'may it bo with the resolution to de
rather than commit a crime!' and I have kept this
injunction in my heart when there seemed no way
of escape except through crime; and, God helping
me, I will keep it to the end."

articles.text:
OUR MISCELLANY.

THE MANNER, IN WHICH ISLANDS ARE

FIRST PLANTED.
The manner in which distant islands become
planted with trees, shrubs, and flowers is exceed-
ingly curious. The Pacific Islands afford instances,
from which the various methods may be successfully
developed. How European and American fruits
came to be naturalized in some of those islands is
sufficiently obvious. Some have been carried
thither by accident; some for delight; and others
for subsistence. Some have been mixed with other
seeds, and thus been transported against the will
and wish of the transporters: as darnel amongst
rye, and millilot amongst wheat. Cook planted
the pineapple and melon in Eooa •, on Christmas
Island yams and COCOAS; on Lefooga, melons,
pumpkins, and Indian corn. Vancouver planted
water-cresses and vine-cuttings in New Holland;
on the Island of Cocos, peas, beaus, apples, melons,
and peach-stones. Captain Colneth had previously
left a variety of garden seeds. On other islands he
had also introduced the almond. Wilson planted
the bread-fruit tree on the Palmerstone Islands.
This tree, so abundant in its useful qualities, is yet
held in little esteem in the islands of India. In
Otaheite successive navigators have introduced
various species of plants and vegetables: and other
islands have been benefited in a similar manner.
But the mode in which these islands became rich
in what we now call- native plants, is a subject of
much difficulty. Let us endeavour to explain it.
One of the circumstances on which Columbus and
his crew founded their hopes of being near land,
was that of the Nigna taking up a branch, the red
berries of which were as fresh as if they had been
taken immediately from the tree. Philips, also, in
his voyage to Botany Bay, saw a great number of
cocoa-nuts floating at a great distance from the
shore. And Captain Tuckey found several patches
of reeds and trees, forty leagues front the African
coast, Near one of the Aleutian Islands Lieutenant
ICotzebue picked up the log of a camphor tree:
and fell in with an iceberg, having a portion of
its surface lined with earth, in which grew trees
and other vegetable substances. There were, also,
the large remains of an animal, which he supposed
to have been the mammoth. The violence of the
floods, too, frequently detach large pieces of land
from the Sumatra shores, which, formed into
islands, float to a groat distance in the sea.
CO-OPERATION OF THE WIFE.
There is much good sense and truth in the
remark of a modern author, that no man ever pros-
pered in the world without the co-operation of his
wife. If she unites in mutual endeavours, or
rewards his labour with a smile, with what con-
fidence will he resort to his merchandise or his
farm—fly over lands, sail upon the sea, meet diffi-
culty or encounter danger—if he knows he is not
spending his strength in vain, but that his labour
will be rewarded by the sweets of home.

AN OLLA PODRIDA.
On entering Spain, the oil and garlic used by
the cooks forced me into starvation; but by de-
grees my fastidiousness vanished, and I became
oven boldienough, before a fortnight had expired,
to taste, without dissatisfaction, the celebrated
" olla podrida," so universally admired in every
province of the Peninsula. This is a sublime
compbund, in the preparation of which all the in-
genuity and genius of a Spanish cook are brought
into requisition; his reputation is staked upon
this die, and upon it is based whatever claims he
may entertain of immortality. Its ingredients are
multifarious, and the mode of mixing them
elaborate and difficult. Two earthenware pots
are generally used, though one is sometimes made
to answer the purpose. In the former case the
different meats—such as a chicken, a slice of beef,
and a piece of bacon—are put together into one of
the vessels, and boiled for a short time over the
fire; they are then allowed to simmer for several
hours. In the other pot or pan the various vege-
tables are collected. These consist of beets,
carrots, beans, peas, onions, celery, garlic, lettuces,
and long pepper; these are likewise permitted to
simmer for four or five hours. Finally the savoury
contents of both utensils are emptied into an error-
mous dish, the meat being placed in the centre,
and the vegetables built up around like the walls
of a city. It is then ready to be placed upon the
table, and worthy of being devoured by monarchs.

EARLY RISING.
I was always an early riser. Happy the man
who is! Every morning day comes to him with a.
virgin's love, full of bloom and purity and fresh-
ness. The youth of nature is contagious, like the
gladness of a happy child. I doubt if any man
can be called old, so long as he is an early riser
and an early walker." And oh, youth !---take my
word for it—youth in dressing gown and slippers,
dawdling over breakfast at noon, is a very deerepid

ghastly image of that youth which sees the sun
blush over the mountains, and the dews sparkling
upon blossoming hedgerows.
HOME QUESTIONS.
_

Did you ever know anybody to stick to any
kind of business, no matter how unpromising, ten
years at most, who did not prosper? Not one!
no matter how bad it might be in the beginning, if
he stuck to it earnestly and faithfully, and tried
nothing else, no matter how hard he found it
sometimes to keep his bead above water, still, if
he persevered, he always came out bright in the
long run—didn't he? Whatever it might have
been at the beginning, at the end of ten years he had
made a business for himself.
LOVING KINDNESS._ a

Let your heart grow cold, and the frost of dis-
trust and bitterness will gather around it, blinding
the soul and shutting out the light; but kindle
up the fires of love, and the windows of the soul
will become as clear as crystal, transmitting the
light of Heaven and giving you glimpses of
Paradise.

articles.title: LOVER LOST BY A KISS.
articles.text:
A LOVER LOST BY A KISS.

•
Art Austrian nobleman, one of the handsomest
and most accomplished young men in Vienna, was
passionately in love with a young girl of almost peer-
lessbeauty. She was the daughter of a man of great
rank and influence at court, and on these considera-
tions, as well as in regard to her charms, she was
followed by a multitude of suitors. She was
lovely aid amiable, and treated them with an
affability which still kept them in her train,
although it was generally known that she had
avowed a predilection for the count, and that pre-
parations were making for their nuptials. The
count was of a refilled mind and delicate sensibility;
be loved her forherself alone—forthe virtues which
he believed dwelt in a beautiful form. Like a
lover of such perfections he approached her with
timidity, and when ho touched her a fire shot
through his veins, that warned him not to invade
the sanctuary of her lips. Such were his feelings,
when one night at the house of his intended father-
in-law, a party of young people were met to cele-
brate a certain festival. Several of the young
lady's rejected suitors were present. Forfeits were
one of the pastimes, and all went on with the
greatest merriment, till the count was commanded
by some one to redeem his glove by saluting the
cheek of his intended bride. The count blushed—
trembled—advanced to his mistress—retre4ted--
advanced again—and at last, with a tremor that
shook every fibre of his frame, with a modest grace
be put to his lips the soft ringlet that played upon
her cheek, and in evident confusion retired to de-
mand his redeemed pledge. His mistress gaily
smiled, and the game went on. One of her rejected
suitors, who was of a merry, unthinking disposi-
tion, was adjudged by the same indiscreet crier of
forfiits, "as his last treat before he hanged
himself," to snatch a kiss from the object of his
recent vows. A lively contest ensued between
the lady and the gentleman,—it lasted for a minute,
when the lady yielded, though in the midst of a
convulsive laugh; and the count had the mortifi-
cation, the agony, to see lips, which his delicate
love would not allow him to touch, kissed with
roughness and repetition by another man, and
one whom he despised. Without a word, he rose
from his chair—left the room, and the house,—
and by that good-natured kiss the fair boast of
Vienna lost her husband and her lover. The count
never saw her more.
